items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable Reading Time: 5 minutes How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable There are events across the entire school/university year for students that cover everything from orientation to graduation, conferences and cultural festivals, sports competitions. These events gather people together, but they also produce extensive waste disposable food containers, printed materials, decorations and single-use supplies for the event. Educational institutions can also lower their carbon footprint by implementing greener practices, because it also teaches students sustainable habits that they will take with them through the rest of their lives after graduation. Sustainable changes to campus events do not necessarily require a large amount of money or radical alterations. Many of the most helpful changes grow out of responsible planning, smart purchasing and greater engagement from the campus community. Think Of Events With Preventive Waste Sustainability needs to be planned in since the earliest stages of planning an event rather than being afterthought once waste is already generated. Organisers can start by estimated attendance, main supplies need to get for use and reference the environmental concern with previous events. Digital registration, electronic invitations and online event schedules are opportunities to eliminate the fabric of waste by cutting out unnecessary paper consumption. For printable materials which are necessary, organizers can print only the copies needed and use double-sided printing when they should be. Also, some schools or universities create sustainability checklists that include catering, transport, energy use and waste management. Clear responsibilities for event teams allow environmentally-sensitive matters to remain part of the planning process. Bottom line prevention from unnecessary consumption tends to work better than fully relying on recycling or disposal systems post-event. Minimize Usage of Single Use Plastics and Disposable Materials But disposable cups, plastic cutlery, food containers and water bottles are other elements of the large waste generated on an important campus meeting. A practical solution would be to offer refill water stations and promote the audience to bring reusable bottles. In places where catering facilities are present, reusable plates, cups and cutleries can take the place of disposable ones. Now when organizing the event, one should count on all the required water, energy as well as cleaning and logistics that are needed to handle reusable items properly. Easily identifiable waste stations are another effective way in which to help participants sort recyclables, general rubbish and food scraps. Such stations would need to mirror local collection and processing facilities available to residents. As there is no appropriate infrastructure, items labelled recyclable or compostable are not necessarily recycled or composted. Prevent unnecessary waste and ensure unavoidable waste is managed properly. Opt For Eco-Friendly Supplies And Materials Another consideration is your event materials. Banners, decorations, name badges, lanyards and exhibition materials are sometimes only used for a limited time before ending up in the bin, even though they can remain in good condition. By selecting durable supplies that can be stored and used again for future events, institutions can minimize this waste. With reusable signage, interchangeable name inserts and returnable badge holders, the need to buy replacements for each event can be limited. Organizers planning student orientations or academic conferences can review the reusable badge and lanyard options available through suppliers such as 4inlanyards when evaluating event identification materials. The broader environmental priority should be to select suitable products, recover them after each event, and reuse them wherever practical. Material composition also matters. Making polyester using recycled PET plastic is a way of reducing the need for virgin polyester, but there are many factors that define the environmental benefits over the whole lifecycle including how it is produced, the length of each product life and end-of-life options. Natural fibres themselves can have environmental impacts involving the cultivation of raw materials, consumption of water, post-harvest processing and transport. Instead of expecting that a single sort of material will always be the most sustainable alternative, institutions should assess durability, practicality, sourcing and end-of-life together. Environmental Initiatives for Campus Catering Food waste is a widespread problem during conferences, student parties and university-wide events. Ordering too much leads to waste, wasting not only the food but also all the resources spent to produce, deliver, and prepare it. By analyzing registration data, organizers can better prepare catering by accurately predicting expected attendance and adapting amounts to the timing of the event. Knowledge, practices and behaviour Change sProviding food that is rich in plant ingredients also can have a positive impact on the environment footprint of catering although this will vary with different components and production methods. Subject to local regulations and food safety and suitability requirements, eligible surplus food may be donated to community groups. Inappropriate collection systems may make even unavoidable food scraps unrecyclable, although these might otherwise be compostable. Institutions can record quantities of food leftovers after an event, which can potentially improve catering estimates for future events and identify sources of recurring waste. Promote Sustainable Transport and EnergyUse Individual travel by car to events over long distances can be a major aspect of the carbon footprint for campus events. Where practical and feasible, universities can promote the use of public transport, walking, cycling and carpooling. Depressingly, taking venues closer to public transport links might also reduce the emissions from travel as well. Energy consumption deserves similar attention. Organizers can have efficient lighting, switch off obsolete equipment, choose rooms according to attendance that are not unnecessarily large and so avoid heating large, empty spaces. Hybrid participation may be appropriate for certain conferences where the reduction in long-distance travel is not outweighed by a disproportionate extra energy use, nor does it exclude people who benefit from attending in person. Such decisions illustrate that event sustainability goes well beyond the materials used on the day. Get Students, Teacher, and the Campus Community Sharing responsibility for being environmentally responsible is what helps sustainable events succeed. Societies on campus, environmental groups, teams from facilities and event volunteers can all help with planning and implementation. They can assist attendees in finding out where they can refill, return reusable items , and sort the waste properly. Student groups can also hold environmental awareness sessions where it explains the reason that such practices are important. Feedback is equally valuable. Holding short post-event surveys can help determine if recycling stations were accessible, if digital materials were available and convenient, and what restatement attendees would support in the future. Participation should remain inclusive. Sustainability programmes must also take account of disabled people, financial inequalities and different access to transport or reusable products. Students engage more in these developments and are likely to continue these routines when practiced. Metrics for Better Future Events Institutions require measurable knowledge to comprehend if their sustainability endeavors are effective. Useful indicators comprise waste generation, food surplus and left over contrary to advice by the industry (i.e.feedback) as well as recovered reusable items and low-impact transportation mode-share. This allows organizers to compare the results of similar events and record which actions made a real difference. It can be something as simple as showing a post-event review that identifies the opportunity to reduce excess orders or enhance waste collection. Environmental reporting should remain transparent. Do not claim that an event is entirely sustainable based on a singular action particularly, as we have seen above where other impacts remain unmeasured or poorly-evaluated. Having a history over time for tracking progress against these targets makes it more likely that schools will set realistic targets and use them to guide decision-making. Final Thoughts Pragmatic choices to reduce waste encouraging printing less, reusing what can be reused again, the selective planning of catering and reducing travel unnecessarily are fundamental ways in making campus buildings and events environmentally sustainable while involving a wider audience on campus. The place to begin can be small steps, monitor outcomes and continuously enhance later on. These initiatives not only lessen environmental impacts but they also create an opportunity to implement practical experience relative to sustainability. Exposure to responsible resource use in everyday campus operations can shape student behavior as they move into their careers and communities. The post How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Service dogs are professionals who are trained to be attentive, helpful and extremely well-behaved for their owners who rely on them for everyday living. They aren’t easily distracted and have solid control over their impulses because their job performance is vital to humans who need them. No one wants a service dog going rogue . But underneath all of that self-control and professionalism, service dogs are still dogs , as an adorable reunion on a Disney cruise ship makes delightfully clear. Ashton McGrady is a content creator who shares her adventures with her Golden Retriever service dog, Forest, who has an affinity for Disney characters. In one video, she shows Forest choosing his own stuffy at a Disney gift shop, even putting the money on the counter to pay for it himself. But another video of Forest being reunited with his favorite character, Pluto, has people the world over feeling his joy vicariously. Watch: The internet could not handle this reunion Ashton calls Forest her “best pal and lifesaver,” and it’s clear from her videos that they make a great team. People loved seeing the good doggo get to let loose and enjoy a romp with Pluto and how the cast member interacted with him as well. “Those dogs are such good pups and work so hard to keep their owners safe, it’s nice to see them play for a bit ” “This is the most golden retriever golden I’ve ever seen “ “i just know the actor under the costume was having the best day ever.” “DID PLUTO WAG HIS OWN TAIL??? This is the best thing I’ve seen all day” “It’s like the Disney hug rule applies to dogs…but it’s play with them until they are done.” The “Disney hug rule” referenced here is an apparently unofficial “rule” that DIsney cast members when dressed in character don’t end a child’s hug until the child let’s go, basically letting the child hug the character as long as they want to. It’s not an actual rule, but it’s a thoughtful practice some cast members use to make sure their young guests don’t leave a character meet disappointed. For Forest, the equivalent is playing until he (or his owner, he’s on the job, after all) decides he’s done. This isn’t the first time Forest has had a touching reunion with Pluto. Ashton shared another video with a similar interaction, it’s clear that Pluto truly is Forest’s bestie. What a service dog actually is Ashton also uses social media to educate people about service dogs, as there are a lot of misunderstandings out there about what service animals are, how they work, and where they are allowed to be. Though service dogs and their owners will often naturally form a bond, a service dog is not a pet; it’s a working animal that assists a person with disabilities or health conditions. In fact, service animals are considered medical equipment, in the same category as a wheelchair or an oxygen tank, and they are allowed to go anywhere the person they are serving would normally be allowed to go, even if other animals are not allowed. As the Americans with Disabilities Act website states: “Under the ADA, State and local governments, businesses, and nonprofit organizations that serve the public generally must allow service animals to accompany people with disabilities in all areas of the facility where the public is allowed to go.” Service dogs are sometimes confused with emotional support animals, but they are not the same thing. Service animals are trained to do specific tasks related to mitigating a person’s disability, which could range from recognizing when their owner is needing medical attention to reminding them to take a medication to guiding them around an obstacle or across a street. How to behave around a service dog There are some guidelines and laws that govern how the general public as well as private businesses should interact with service animals. First, no one should pet a service animal unless their handler specifically invites them to. Second, there are only two questions a business owner or their staff members are allowed to ask a person with a service dog: 1) Is the dog a service animal who is required because of a disability? And 2) What work or task has the dog been trained to perform? They are not allowed to ask for documentation, ask what disability the person has or ask that the dog demonstrate what they can do. For people who need them, service animals like Forest are a vital part of living a full life. They are also working professionals who deserve a break now and then, so it’s fun to see this good doggo having the time of his life with his buddy, Pluto. You can follow Ashton on TikTok and YouTube . This article originally appeared lazt year. It has been updated. items.descriptionOriginal: Trees are essential in most neighborhoods. They provide shade, beauty, and places for kids to climb . They also absorb rainwater, help prevent flooding, filter toxins from the air, and are one of the most important ways to fight climate change . Trees play a tremendous role in creating safe and comfortable communities, so caring for them, as they do for us, is paramount. But most of us aren’t arborists and don’t know how to support trees so they stay healthy. A new app used in Berlin, called the Gieß den Kiez project , which means “Water Your Neighborhood” in English, is the first step toward alerting the average person when local trees are thirsty. Kennt ihr "Gieß den Kiez“? Auf der Website von CityLab könnt ihr sehen, welche Bäume in eurer Umgebung Wasser benötigen. https://t.co/1gxouQYWdc pic.twitter.com/dmAIfFA9cw — competence & more (@competencemore) August 19, 2020 People care about trees, but they don’t always know how to help “I was really surprised at just how deeply people care about trees—for many people it’s almost like caring for a pet,” Anna Mehrländer, who has led the Gieß den Kiez project for more than a year, told The Guardian . “Climate change is happening on our doorsteps. But watering a tree is a small action that helps your neighborhood cope as summers get hotter. It also creates community at a time when people are increasingly working from home and on their phones all day.” The app gives users a map of Berlin with 900,000 trees they can adopt. Adoptive tree parents get real-time alerts when it’s time to water the tree, based on weather data, its age, species, and location. When an adopted tree turns from a green dot to a red dot, it’s time to grab a watering can and get to work. Unser Dev-Team ist heute beim #BerlinWaterHackathon und macht Gieß den Kiez fit für den Frühling ! Wir arbeiten an neuen Features und Verbesserungen, z.B. individuelle Baum-Routings, Geolocating für App-Nutzer*innen, Stacked Bar Charts & schickere Pumpen-Layer. pic.twitter.com/ufgiwrVi1N — CityLAB Berlin (@citylabberlin) January 26, 2021 The app’s developers want people to take care of the trees in their neighborhood like they do their pets. But unlike a dog, a tree can’t tell you when it’s thirsty. With this app, neighbors can keep their favorite trees hydrated, and healthier trees mean healthier communities. “It feels very fun, almost like a video game,” Amanda Gläser-Bligh, a Berliner who uses the app, told The Guardian . “I think many people may want to water the trees, but they might feel weird about doing it, or they’re not sure if it’s their responsibility. But if you have this app encouraging you, you know it’s the right thing to do.” Berlin beyond the trees. Photo credit: Canva Over 12,000 people have already signed up The great thing about Gieß den Kiez is that it’s an open-source app, so just about any city in the world can use it, and over 12,000 people have already signed up. Beyond Berlin, it’s keeping trees hydrated in German cities such as Potsdam, Leipzig, and Magdeburg. A version of the platform also operates in Paris’s 17th arrondissement. As temperatures rise, healthy trees have become even more important. A recent Environmental Protection Agency review of 308 studies found that urban areas with forest cover are 3°F cooler than urban areas without greenery. The Gieß den Kiez experiment reminds us that countless people want to care for the environment and their communities. But often, they just don’t know where to start. Giving people a specific job and letting them know when to act is a great way to turn anyone into a steward of urban forestry. items.titleOriginal: This Woman Is Keeping Bengal’s Alpona Art Alive
items.description: Στις 5 το πρωί, ενώ η Καλκούτα κοιμάται, μια 74χρονη γυναίκα είναι απασχολημένη να σκορπίζει την ευτυχία, ένα κατώφλι τη φορά. Γνωρίστε τον Ratnabali Ghosh, γνωστό στοργικά ως Alpona Didi της Καλκούτα. Κάθε χρόνο, λίγο πριν από το Diwali, βγαίνει νωρίς το πρωί για να ζωγραφίσει όμορφα παραδοσιακά alponas έξω από τα σπίτια αγνώστων, μετατρέποντας τα συνηθισμένα κατώφλια σε συγκινητική έκπληξη…
items.descriptionOriginal: At 5 AM, while Kolkata sleeps, a 74-year-old woman is busy spreading happiness, one doorstep at a time. Meet Ratnabali Ghosh, lovingly known as Kolkata’s Alpona Didi. Every year, just before Diwali, she steps out early in the morning to paint beautiful traditional alponas outside strangers’ homes, turning ordinary doorsteps into heartwarming surprises. For elderly residents living away from their children, these intricate patterns mean much more than art. They bring a sense of connection, care, and the comforting feeling that someone is thinking of them. Through this simple yet beautiful gesture, Ratnabali is keeping Bengal’s traditional alpona art alive while bringing smiles to people across Kolkata. Her story reminds us that making a difference doesn’t always require grand gestures. Sometimes, a little kindness can brighten someone’s entire day. ❤️ What is one small act of kindness that has stayed with you? Watch Ratnabali Ghosh’s full story on YouTube ➡️ https://youtu.be/O87taxrk_aM ⁠￼ 🎥 @ratnabali.ghosh #RatnabaliGhosh #AlponaDidi #AlponaArt #Kolkata #BengaliCulture #BengaliTradition #TraditionalIndianArt #Diwali #IndianCulture #ActsOfKindness #InspiringStories #WomenWhoInspire #CulturalHeritage #PositiveIndia #thebetterindia

items.title: Πώς ο μισθός 4000 Rs/μήνα και μια δουλειά πίσω από την κάμερα ξεκίνησαν το ταξίδι του Nani στο "Natural Star"
items.titleOriginal: How Rs 4000/Month Salary & a Job Behind the Camera Started Nani’s Journey to ‘Natural Star’
items.description: «Μου δόθηκε σε χαρτονομίσματα των 100 Rs και θυμάμαι ότι τα ένιωθα στην τσέπη μου καθώς πήγαινα με το ποδήλατό μου πίσω στο σπίτι». Έτσι περιέγραψε ο Νάνι τον πρώτο του μισθό ως βοηθός σκηνοθέτη σε μια συνέντευξη που επισκέφτηκε αργότερα ο Κοίμος, και το ποσό ήταν 4.000 Rs. Είπε ότι ένιωθε αρκετά πλούσιος εκείνο το βράδυ για να φανταστεί ότι αγόραζε το μισό Χαϊντεραμπάντ. Σήμερα, ο άνθρωπος που μετράει…
items.descriptionOriginal: "It was given to me in Rs 100 notes, and I remember feeling them in my pocket as I rode my bike back home." That is how Nani described his first salary as an assistant director in an interview Koimoi later revisited, and the sum was Rs 4,000. He has said he felt rich enough that evening to imagine buying half of Hyderabad. Today, the man who counted those notes is Telugu cinema's Natural Star, an actor whom audiences describe as one of the industry's most relatable, and his road there began far from any spotlight. Learning cinema from behind the camera Born Ghanta Naveen Babu in Hyderabad, Nani did not set out to act. Inspired by filmmaker Mani Ratnam , he wanted to direct, and producer Anil Kumar Koneru let him join the sets of Radha Gopalam (2005) as a clap assistant. He then worked as an assistant director on Allari Bullodu, Dhee and Asthram , learning how a film comes together one shot at a time. Nani spent about a year as a radio jockey, hosting Non-Stop Nani before an advertisement led to his acting debut in Ashta Chamma in 2008. Photograph: ( India Today ) But before the camera found him, a microphone did. A friend working at WorldSpace Satellite Radio offered him a job as a radio jockey , and he spent about a year hosting a programme called Non-Stop Nani. According to The Times of India, the show made his voice familiar to listeners, although acting remained his greater ambition. The films that put Nani on the map In 2008, director Mohana Krishna Indraganti noticed Nani in an advertisement and cast him in Ashta Chamma , which gave him his lead-acting debut. The romantic comedy, a free adaptation of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest , was released on 5 September 2008 and earned Rs 6 crore as the distributors' share, so the newcomer arrived with a success behind him. Ride (2009) and Bheemili Kabaddi Jattu (2010), a remake of the Tamil film Vennila Kabadi Kuzhu, kept the momentum going, with the latter becoming a surprise hit. Snehituda (2009) did not succeed, yet Nani kept getting lead roles, and in 2012 he won the Nandi Award for Best Actor for Yeto Vellipoyindhi Manasu , directed by Gautham Vasudev Menon. Ala Modalaindi , a 2011 romantic comedy directed by Nandini Reddy, became his breakthrough. In 2012, S S Rajamouli cast him in Eega , where Nani's character returns as a fly to take revenge on the man who wronged him. The film earned over Rs 125 crore and won two National Film Awards, which showed how willingly Nani backed ambitious ideas. How he became the 'Natural Star' The nickname arrived with Bhale Bhale Magadivoy in 2015. It was one of the few small-budget Telugu films to cross US$1 million at the box office, and it became the first blockbuster of his career. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor in Telugu for it, and audiences began calling him the Natural Star because his performances felt so unforced. In S S Rajamouli's Eega (2012), Nani played a man who returns as a fly to seek revenge, taking on an unconventional role early in his career. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) What kept the title alive was the kind of person he chose to play. His characters are flawed people working through love, ambition, family and the uncertainties of ordinary life, so viewers tend to see themselves in them. In Jersey (2019), he played a former cricketer who returns to the game for the sake of his young son, a performance that Film Companion placed on its list of the 100 greatest performances of the decade. In Hi Nanna (2023), he played a fashion photographer raising his daughter alone, and the film became a commercial success. He also took risks with the image he had built. V (2020), his 25th film and first OTT release, cast him as a serial killer, his first negative role, and it became the most-watched Telugu film on streaming, according to Wikipedia's account of his career. The honours followed. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award again for Shyam Singha Roy , which made him the only Telugu actor to win it twice. In 2024, he took home his first Filmfare Award for Best Actor in Telugu for Dasara at the 69th Filmfare Awards South, where he was also nominated for Hi Nanna. His next project, The Paradise , reunites him with Dasara director Srikanth Odela. For an actor who once measured success in a pocketful of Rs 100 notes, the journey suggests a career can be built one opportunity at a time, through patience, a willingness to try unusual roles, and a gift for looking like someone the audience already knows. items.descriptionOriginal: With fuel prices sky-high, the need for fuels from non-petroleum sources has taken on a new urgency. And researchers at Worchester Polytechnic Institute say they might have just the alternative source we need for low-carbon and low-cost fuel: bamboo. Bamboo could power trains, planes, and automobiles for as little as $2.75 per gasoline-gallon equivalent at mature commercial scale, the researchers calculate. The fuel would emit greenhouse gas emissions 26 times lower than conventional diesel fuel. What’s more, bamboo promises to be a more sustainable biofuel feedstock than conventional ones like corn and sugarcane. Bamboo is a grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some species growing several dozen inches in a day. Because of this fast growth rate, the US could make as much fuel from bamboo as it makes ethanol from corn while using about 13% as much land . The WPI researchers published their results in the journal Sustainable Energy & Fuels . “I think this research is especially timely and important because fuel prices are high and the transportation sector produces more greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. than any other,” said chemical engineering professor Michael Timko in a press release . “Bamboo would use different land than we are using for food production, so there is no food versus fuel trade-off. Farmers win, consumers win.” .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: How sustainable are aviation biofuels really? Timko and colleagues evaluated bamboo for biofuel production using a process called hydrothermal liquefaction. In the process, wet biomass or organic wastes are subjected to high heat and pressure. Polymer chains in the mass breaks down to form a biocrude oil. The oil can then be converted to other liquid fuel products. The researchers heated wet bamboo pulp to 300°C for 10 minutes. The process converted about 36% of its mass into biocrude. Unlike corn or sugarcane, which are the main plants used to make biofuels today , bamboo wouldn’t compete with agricultural land and doesn’t need much water or energy to grow. And compared with other perennial grasses that are also being considered for biofuel, it has very low ash content—less than 1% by weight—so the fuel-making process generates minimal waste. ”Bamboo may eventually offer industry a way to generate low-carbon liquid fuels at scale,” Timko said. Source : Timothy M. Woodard et al. Bamboo as a cost-effective feedstock for production of low carbon transportation fuels. Sustainable Energy & Fuels , 2026. Οι μέρες της περιστρέφονταν γύρω από τις δουλειές του σπιτιού, την κτηνοτροφία, τις αγροτικές εργασίες και τη φροντίδα των παιδιών της. Στην κοινότητά της, οι γυναίκες είχαν λίγες ευκαιρίες να παρακολουθήσουν συναντήσεις έξω από το h…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with S M Sehgal Foundation. For 26-year-old Anchal of Hussaini village, leaving home for a meeting was once difficult to imagine. Her days revolved around household chores, livestock, farm work and caring for her children. In her community, women had few opportunities to attend meetings outside their homes or speak to people from the village. So when she decided to join the Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise in Chhata block of Mathura in 2023, the first hurdle was at home. "They felt that the women of the house should not go out and work," she recalls. It was not an easy argument to make. Anchal had a household to run and three children to care for, two of whom have disabilities and need regular treatment. But staying at home had begun to weigh on her. "I was confined at home, and getting stressed. I wanted to do something of my own," she says. Nearly three years later, Anchal is part of the team running the mustard oil unit in her village. She earns around Rs 5,000-6,000 a month and contributes towards her children's treatment. But to get there, she first had to find a way to step outside a life that had largely been defined for her. The first hurdle was at home Anchal had completed her bachelor of arts after studying up to Class 12 in her village. Yet her education had not translated into work outside the home. "I didn't want to be confined to the house. I was waiting for a chance to step out and work," she says. Her family did not agree immediately. She had to convince them that she could work while continuing to care for her children and manage the household. She began waking early to finish her chores before leaving for the unit. The Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise was set up in 2023 with a total investment of Rs 14 lakh. Anchal joined the enterprise in November 2023. Her mother-in-law takes care of the children while she is away, and Anchal returns early whenever they need her. Joining the enterprise changed more than her daily routine. She had also been uncomfortable speaking to anyone outside her immediate circle. "Earlier, we couldn't speak freely with anyone outside our community. We hardly had any contact with outsiders," she says. That changed once she began working at the unit, alongside women she had never had any reason to speak with before. 'I was just looking for a chance to work' Preeti, now 32, arrived at the enterprise from a different starting point. Originally from Haryana, she moved to Hussaini after marriage. She had completed her bachelor of arts and taught children at schools in her village for around three years. Her father had also taught her tailoring and encouraged her to become self-reliant. After marriage, however, her days became centred on the household, cattle and fields. "I was always looking for a chance to work somewhere," she says. The opportunity came through the Shri Ji self-help group, which is linked to the National Rural Livelihoods Mission. When S M Sehgal Foundation began discussing a mustard oil unit in Hussaini around January-February 2023, Preeti became involved. But like Anchal, she first had to convince her family. Her in-laws worried about women working outside the home, what people might say and whether they could be exploited. Preeti asked her husband to come and see the work for himself before deciding. "I wanted him to understand what I was doing before I stepped out to work. If he was comfortable, I would take the chance," she says. He eventually supported her and helped convince his parents. Preeti also helped prepare the space for the enterprise , including arranging money for the electrical connection through contributions from home and their milkman. The women were ready to work. The next challenge was getting the enterprise itself off the ground. Before production, they had to win trust The Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise was set up in 2023 with a total investment of Rs 14 lakh. Of this, Rs 8 lakh came through the S M Sehgal Foundation's project supported by HDFC Bank Parivartan, while Rs 6 lakh was mobilised as community contribution, largely in kind. The idea emerged after a survey found that families in the area widely used mustard oil. Given the Foundation's existing work with local women, the team felt the women could run the enterprise on their own. Not everyone agreed. Chhaya Singh, 36, a field specialist in data and documentation at S M Sehgal Foundation, has worked closely with the enterprise for the past three years. She remembers village elders suggesting that the project be handed to men instead. "They believed women could not do it. That only made us more determined to prove them wrong," she says. For Chhaya, the goal was always for the women to take charge of the enterprise themselves. "We wanted women to be part of an enterprise, but more importantly, we wanted them to run it themselves," she says. "We also wanted them to see what is possible and help other women get the same opportunities." The machine at the centre of it all — an expeller that crushes mustard seeds to extract oil — was initially unfamiliar to all of them. For five to six months, the team met regularly with the women's family members, explaining what the enterprise involved and making the case for why the women were capable of running it. Once that groundwork was done, the team trained the women in financial literacy, stock management, and technical skills to prepare them for the work ahead. Five women now run the whole unit For Anchal, even approaching the mustard oil machine initially felt intimidating. "At first, I was afraid to even touch the mustard oil machine. I had never worked with anything like it before. But slowly, I learnt, and today I can run it on my own," she tells The Better India. With training from a technical expert, she learnt to operate the machine, understand the demand, track prices, and work through different stages of production. Preeti learnt the technical side too. "I learnt all the work in just 10 to 15 days because the team was always there to guide and support me," she says. The machine at the centre of it all — an expeller that crushes mustard seeds to extract oil — was initially unfamiliar to all of them. Eight women received technical training from an expert who supplied the expeller unit. The five women who run the enterprise today were among them. They learnt every step of the process, from handling mustard seeds to filtering the oil, filling and capping bottles, and even resolving voltage issues on their own. S M Sehgal Foundation supported the unit during its initial years and gradually stepped back as the women took on greater responsibility. How the women run the business today The unit is run by the Shri Ji self-help group, and decisions are taken collectively. Five women associated with this unit since its inception run the enterprise today. Kavita, the president, coordinates the group, reviews accounts, leads meetings and works on market linkages. Preeti, the treasurer, handles accounts, expenditure and cash flow. Anchal, the secretary, oversees operations, maintains registers and tracks stock, receives visitors and participates in decisions. Bati cleans mustard seeds and extracts oil , while Ritu handles filtration, filling, sealing, labelling and packaging. Between January and August 2026, the women sold 2,995.5 litres of mustard oil and 3,841.5 kg of oil cake. Their market now extends beyond Hussaini and neighbouring villages to Kosi Kalan town in Chhata block of Mathura district, as well as Mathura, Aligarh and Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh; Gurugram, Faridabad, Palwal and Hodal in Haryana; and parts of Rajasthan. According to the Foundation's latest figures, the enterprise generated Rs 6,53,980 in sales between January and August 2026. Since beginning commercial operations in November 2023, its cumulative sales have crossed Rs 24 lakh. Five percent is set aside for maintenance, and the remaining amount is divided equally among the five members. If someone does not need her share immediately, it can remain with the group and be lent to another member at one percent interest. 'Money has given me stability' For Preeti, the biggest changes can be seen outside the unit too. She has travelled for meetings in Uttarakhand, Mathura and Chhata. She contributes towards her children's school fees and household expenses and is able to save some money herself. Her family now sees her work differently. Her mother-in-law, who was initially unsure about her stepping outside the home, now cooks with the oil the enterprise produces and has come to rely on Preeti's earnings too. Even with that growing support, Preeti still seeks her in-laws' permission before visiting other people's homes. She hopes this will change with time. S M Sehgal Foundation supported the unit during its initial years and gradually stepped back as the women took on greater responsibility. For Anchal, earning has changed how she can contribute at home. Before she began working, she had to depend on her husband's income for purchases. Today, she can share those expenses, including the ongoing care her two children with disabilities need. "Earlier, my husband had to manage every expense on his own. Now, I can share that responsibility. If my children need medicines, I don't have to wait or depend on him to buy them," she says. "My biggest wish is to see my children get better. I am ready to work as hard as I have to if it can help make that happen," she says. What the work looks like beyond Hussaini The Hussaini enterprise sits within a wider network of women involved in S M Sehgal Foundation's work. The organisation has worked with rural communities for 28 years, focusing on skills, market connections and helping communities manage enterprises themselves. In Maharashtra, women in Nanda Agade's self-help group, who previously worked as farm labourers, now run a Custom Hiring Centre with its own tractor. The initiative has reduced annual rental costs by Rs 4 to 5 lakh. In Kolar, Karnataka, 389 women are shareholders in the Laxmisagara Horticulture Farmer Producer Company. 'I have a lot of hope for this enterprise' Anchal hopes to see another enterprise come up in Hussaini one day, giving other women the same chance to work and earn that she had. But her children remain at the centre of what she wants for the future. For Preeti, earning more is tied to the opportunities she hopes to give her children. She wants them to receive the best education possible and dreams of seeing them become teachers, following a path she once envisioned for herself. This is also part of why she has begun thinking about the future of her enterprise, as its growth will shape the opportunities she can provide for her children. "I have a lot of hope for this enterprise. I want to see it grow stronger so that all of us women can run it confidently on our own," she says. Both women came to the unit with fairly simple wishes. Anchal wanted space beyond a home life. Preeti wanted work that felt like her own. Both also needed an income of their own: Anchal for her children's treatment, and Preeti for school fees and household expenses. The unit is run by the Shri Ji self-help group, and decisions are taken collectively. Since then, both women have challenged what their families once thought possible for them. They have learnt to operate unfamiliar machinery, taken on responsibilities they once had little opportunity to pursue, and grown more confident in making decisions for themselves. Today, when mustard arrives at the unit , the women collectively know how much to buy, how to run the machine, how to keep the accounts, how to fill and seal the bottles and how to speak with customers. And when a decision has to be made, the women sit together and make it. All pictures courtesy S M Sehgal Foundation.

items.description: Οι μέλισσες σπρώχνουν επιθετικά τους άγριους επικονιαστές μακριά από τα λουλούδια, με τους επιστήμονες να καταγράφουν πώς διώχνουν τους αντιπάλους τους και κυριαρχούν σε πολύτιμες πηγές τροφής. items.descriptionOriginal: Honeybees are aggressively pushing wild pollinators away from flowers, with scientists documenting how they chase off rivals and dominate valuable food sources. items.descriptionOriginal: For Kalpana, a woman artisan in Andhra Pradesh's Chinnapuram village, something that once clogged local waterways has become a source of income. She works with water hyacinth, an invasive plant that spreads rapidly across canals and ponds. Once removed, it was usually thrown away. Today, women like Kalpana are turning it into handbags, baskets, lampshades and other products people can use at home. "This work needs skill and dedication. Every product we make carries our effort and creativity," Kalpana told The New Indian Express . She reported earning around Rs 500 to Rs 700 a day from the craft. And she is part of a growing effort that has trained around 150 women across Andhra Pradesh's Krishna district to earn from a plant long considered a nuisance. How did a troublesome weed become a livelihood? For years, water hyacinth has troubled Krishna district's canals and water bodies. The fast-growing plant forms thick mats across the water, blocking movement and making it difficult to keep canals clear. Irrigation workers would remove it, only for the weed to grow back. But what if the material being discarded could be put to use? In October 2024, the Krishna district administration launched a training programme in Chinnapuram village, Machilipatnam mandal, to help women from self-help groups learn the craft of making products from water hyacinth. The initiative began with 50 women and involved experienced artisans from Assam, including national award-winning craftsperson Rita Das and her team. During the initial training phase, approximately 100–120 tonnes of water hyacinth were removed each month. Photograph: (newsmeter) The women learnt how to collect, dry, weave and finish the plant into products suitable for sale. The process requires patience. Once collected, the water hyacinth is dried in the sun for nearly 15 days. Its dried stalks are then woven by hand into different shapes, followed by gumming and polishing to give the finished products strength and a smooth appearance. During training, participants received an allowance of Rs 300 a day. Today, the Chinnapuram artisans produce around 50 to 60 varieties of handicrafts, including storage containers, mats, trays, handbags and decorative items. The women have also formed a society called Hyaloom to manage orders, production and income sharing. According to a February 2026 report by The New Indian Express , artisans in the group were earning an average of Rs 10,000 to Rs 15,000 a month, with earnings varying according to demand. From one village to 150 trained women What began in Chinnapuram has since expanded to other villages across Krishna district, including Chevendra, Leelagudem and Tamirisa. By September 2026, around 150 women had received training under the initiative. And the results extend beyond the products they make. During the initial training phase, approximately 100 to 120 tonnes of water hyacinth were being removed every month. With growing orders, the programme now has the capacity to handle around 150 tonnes monthly in the areas covered. According to The Times of India , the initiative has generated approximately Rs 20 lakh in combined sales and earnings, with an estimated margin of 20% after expenses, including labour charges. The products are reaching buyers through Lepakshi, which has been supporting their marketing. The district administration is also exploring opportunities with major temples, including those at Srikalahasti, Srisailam and Kanaka Durga. Women in Andhra Pradesh are converting water hyacinth into eco-friendly products, creating steady incomes while restoring local water bodies. A powerful blend of sustainability, innovation and women-led growth. 🌿✨ #AndhraPradesh #SustainableLivelihoods #EcoInnovation #WomenEmpowerment — Andhra Community (@AndhraCommunity) February 1, 2026 Even the organic manure produced through the process is finding buyers among local farmers. The next challenge is ensuring that women continue receiving orders. "The next priority is to provide regular orders and sustainable market opportunities to the trained women," Y Hari Hara Nath, project director of the District Rural Development Agency, told The Times of India . The administration hopes to expand the programme to the district's remaining 20 mandals. For women like Kalpana, the change is already meaningful. A weed that once had to be cleared and discarded is now something they can shape with their own hands and sell. And with each new order, the skills they have learnt offer another opportunity to earn. Sources: 'Women in Krishna district turn water hyacinth into source of livelihood' : By Vidya Dusi, Published on 26 September 2026 'Women turn water hyacinth into livelihood' : By Y Brahmaji, Published on 1 February 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Battery-Like Technology Offers a New Path for Capturing Carbon Dioxide Reading Time: 3 minutes A new battery-like technology developed by University of Illinois and Toyota engineers pulls carbon dioxide straight out of open air using electricity instead of heat. A new battery-like device can now pull carbon dioxide straight out of the air. Engineers built it by borrowing tricks from rechargeable battery technology. The approach could make direct air capture cheaper and easier to scale. Researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built the device with Toyota. Their findings appear in the journal Environmental Science & Technology. The team says its method could outperform existing direct air capture (DAC) systems. Mechanical engineering professor Kyle Smith led the Illinois side of the project. Graduate students Paul Rozzi and JeongA Lee also contributed to the design and testing. Toyota researchers Chip Roberts and Tim Arthur rounded out the collaborative team. Cutting emissions alone likely will not meet global climate targets. Scientists say some carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere must also be removed. Doing it directly from open air, though, remains technically difficult and costly. Fossil fuel use keeps climbing worldwide, even as renewable energy expands rapidly. That trend makes atmospheric carbon removal an increasingly urgent complement to emissions cuts. A cheaper battery-like device could help close that gap faster. Most carbon capture technology targets concentrated sources like factory smokestacks. Open air contains far less carbon dioxide per breath than smokestack exhaust. Current DAC systems rely on giant fans and costly materials to make up the difference. Smith and his colleagues describe this diluted atmospheric carbon as a legacy problem. Decades of past emissions remain mixed into the air at very low concentrations. Addressing that backlog requires tools built specifically for open-air conditions, not smokestacks. Battery-like technology designed for open-air conditions rather than factory smokestacks addresses what researchers call a legacy problem, targeting the decades of past emissions now diluted across the atmosphere at concentrations too low for conventional direct air capture systems to handle cost-effectively. Photo by Nikita Belokhonov on Pexels. Those materials also need heating once they have soaked up enough carbon dioxide. That step releases the gas for storage or reuse elsewhere. Heating adds significant energy costs to the whole process. The new battery-like technology skips heat altogether. It relies on an electrochemical cell built from specialized manganese dioxide electrodes. A saltwater solution flows through the cell during operation. Running current in one direction makes the solution more alkaline. That alkaline solution readily absorbs carbon dioxide from the surrounding air. Reversing the current makes the solution less alkaline, releasing pure carbon dioxide for capture. This alkaline shift allows carbon dioxide to dissolve far more readily than in neutral water. Researchers describe the setup as a cation-compensated cell built around proton-intercalation electrodes. That design keeps the whole cycle reversible, much like charging and discharging a battery. Similar electrode materials already appear in some rechargeable battery designs. Applying that same chemistry to carbon capture is part of what makes this approach unusual. It also helps explain why the team compares the device’s operation to a battery. Early lab results already look encouraging for the new method. Researchers still need to prevent the device’s two liquid streams from mixing. Solving that problem should improve both energy use and overall capture efficiency. Toyota Motor North America helped fund the research alongside university grants. The University of Illinois has filed patent applications, with Toyota holding joint rights. Toyota describes the work as part of its broader push toward long-term decarbonization. Additional support came from the university’s Campus Research Board and Grainger College of Engineering. That mix of industry and academic funding is common for early-stage climate technology. Researchers say continued support will be needed to move the device beyond the lab. Full details of the study appear in a University of Illinois news release describing the project. Battery-like technology like this one add a new option to a still-young field. Some direct air capture methods use heat, while others use chemical filters instead. Electricity-driven designs like this one could offer a cheaper path toward pulling old carbon back out of the sky. Wider testing outside the lab will show whether that promise holds up at scale. For now, the results mark a hopeful early step for a technology the world will likely need. The post Battery-Like Technology Offers a New Path for Capturing Carbon Dioxide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: O ne weekend, a canvasser — let’s call her Cindy — was out door-knocking and found a gentleman at home. After establishing that he’d heard of gender transition surgeries for minors, a topic that’s become a major focal point across the U.S. in the run-up to the midterm elections, Cindy asked him where on a scale of zero to 10 his views were, where zero meant he was against banning procedures for minors and 10 meant he was in favor of the ban. “I’d be about an eight,” said the man. Let’s call him Ethan. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “About an Eight” Then ensued an open-hearted conversation during which Ethan admitted he thinks minors don’t always know what’s best and Cindy divulged that she is transgender. She went on to share her experience of how she had come to recognize she was trans — how she had felt like she was wearing a costume that didn’t fit. “I actually like clothes now, which is crazy,” she said. “Now I get to just pick something that’s me.” “Good!” Ethan replied. “That’s good.” Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “A Costume That Didn’t Fit” Only towards the end of their conversation did they get back to the ballot measure. Cindy explained that gender-affirming care for minors typically follows a multi-stage, developmentally-paced model, starting with visits to doctors and counselors with family in tow, and then “social transition,” where individuals change their name and pronouns. Personal storytelling and active listening, rather than debate, are at the heart of deep canvassing. Credit: JJ Lane / Be Lovely Photography Only then can they start taking puberty pausing medication, which is reversible, and after a couple years of that, usually from the age of 18, they can begin taking hormones to go through the puberty that aligns with how they want to live their life. “I wish that I had been able to access this kind of care when I was younger,” Cindy said. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “I Only Have One Go-Around” At this point, she asked Ethan where he would now put himself on the scale they’d discussed at the start. “I’d probably be more like a three,” Ethan said. “Boy, you gonna have me thinking the rest of the day. I probably won’t sleep tonight!” Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “About a Three” Cindy and Ethan, canvasser and voter, are engaged in what’s known as deep canvassing, a technique of going door-to-door where the canvasser does more listening than talking. The idea is to have an open-minded, non-judgmental conversation about a hot-button issue, be it abortion, trans rights or mass deportations, and have the canvasser share their own vulnerabilities while asking questions about the voter’s life. The hope is to connect on an emotional level and find out what’s really going on for folks. The post The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Come winter, a typical Bengali turns romantic about nolen gur. This fresh jaggery is made from the sap of the wild date palm (Phoenix sylvestris) and is usually available from mid-November to February. The love comes in many versions. There is liquid jaggery, warm and fragrant . There are chhanagolla (cottage cheese balls) shaped in the freshest gur. If we are feeling indulgent, there is a thin, flaky paratha to go with a bowl of jhola (nolen) gur. For all that, I would still choose a crisp slice of toast with nolen gur. Literature romanticised it too. In Bhalo Rey Bhalo, the pioneering Bengali writer and poet Sukumar Ray celebrates life's many pleasures, from the fragrance of flowers to the cottony blooms of the shimul tree. Few of them, he suggests, can rival eating nolen gur with bread. It belongs as much to memory as to the kitchen. But it has a constraint that sugar and many other sweeteners do not. It can only be made when the weather, the tree and the sap align. That gives Bengal a short winter window to make the most of it. Why the window is so short The window is set by temperature, the chemistry of the sap, and how quickly it can be harvested and processed before it ferments. Fermentation is the clock. Fresh palm sap contains fermentable sugars, which microorganisms can begin converting into alcohol and organic acids. As fermentation progresses, the sap's acidity, sweetness and other properties change, and so does its suitability for jaggery-making . A 1988 study by T R Shamala and K R Sreekantiah, published in Food Microbiology, identified yeasts, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and several types of bacteria in freshly tapped wild date-palm sap. The researchers documented changes in microbial growth and in the production of ethanol, acids and esters during fermentation. Their findings help explain why freshly collected sap cannot be left standing for long before processing. Cooler winter conditions help slow fermentation, giving tappers a better chance of collecting usable sap. Photograph: (Indrajit Lahiri/moha-mushkil) Cold buys time. Cooler winter conditions slow fermentation and give tappers a better chance of collecting usable sap. Once the weather warms, that window becomes harder to manage. The sap must be brought down early and processed promptly to preserve the qualities nolen gur needs. Even within winter, the sap keeps changing. A 2015 study in the Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences looked at this in Bengal itself. Dipak Girhepuje, S Mondal and P K Bandopadhyay of Bidhan Chandra Krishi Viswavidyalaya examined sap from 15-to-20-year-old trees in Haringhata block, Nadia district. They took separate samples between December and February across two seasons, 2012–13 and 2013–14. Their findings: Total soluble solids, which indicate the concentration of dissolved substances, reached 14.33% in February. Total sugar rose from 11.37% in December to 12.50% in February. The sugar-to-acid ratio fell sharply, from 325.47 in January to 42.93 in February. Vitamin C declined from 18.75 mg per 100 ml in December to 13.75 mg in February. Alcohol content was highest in February. So the sap does not stay chemically identical through winter. Its properties shift even within the traditional harvesting period. How nolen gur is made Before Kolkata's sweet shops fill their trays with nolen gur sandesh, and before we get the first taste, a lot happens in villages across Bankura, Birbhum, Jhargram and Khejuri (Purba Medinipur). The night a tree fills a pot. The process begins with the khejur gaach, or date palm. Traditional tappers, known as shiuli or siuli, make a controlled incision in the tree and fit a small bamboo channel to guide the sap into an earthen pot. The pot hangs overnight and collects the liquid that flows from the cut. In the hours before dawn, the tapper returns to the tree he climbed the previous evening and lowers the pot. The timing is essential, for the reasons above. When the sap meets the fire. Freshly collected sap is not yet jaggery. It is filtered and heated in large pans so that water evaporates and the sugars concentrate. As the liquid thickens, its colour, viscosity and flavour change. The result may be jhola gur, a pourable jaggery, or patali gur, the solid variety used in sweets. For sweet-makers, the quality of the finished jaggery depends on both the sap they receive and how carefully it is processed. Photograph: (Sabyasachi/foodaholix) A 2009 study in the Journal of Food Engineering examined this transformation. P V K Jagannadha Rao, Madhusweta Das and S K Das studied how boiling changes the physical properties of sugarcane, palmyra-palm and date-palm juices. As dissolved solids increased, the juices became more viscous and their boiling temperatures rose. For date-palm juice, the changes were particularly pronounced in the final stage of concentration. For sweet-makers, this means the quality of the finished jaggery depends on both the sap they receive and how carefully it is processed. More than a seasonal sweet Nolen gur connects Bengal's winter landscape to its food traditions and rural livelihoods. It gives pithe, payesh and sandesh their seasonal character. It also supports the people whose knowledge of trees, tapping and boiling makes it possible. That dependence on winter has consequences. As warmer weather threatens to shorten the tapping season, producers face declining yields, and sweet-makers face uncertain supplies of an ingredient central to the winter table. A shorter winter can mean fewer litres of sap, less jaggery to sell and a smaller income from months of specialised work. Preserving nolen gur therefore means looking beyond the sweet shops. It means understanding how changing temperatures affect the date palm's harvesting cycle, documenting changes in sap yields over time, and supporting the tappers whose livelihoods rest on a narrow winter window. As climate change reshapes seasonal patterns, the challenge is to safeguard the ecological conditions and traditional knowledge that make nolen gur possible. Sources: 'Microbiological and biochemical studies on traditional Indian palm wine fermentation' : By T.R Shamala, K.R Sreekantiah, Published on 20 October 2004 'Changes in physico-chemical properties of wild date palm (Phoenix sylvestris) sap over its peak production period' : Dipak Girhepuje, S Mondal and P K Bandopadhyay, Published on 8 July 2015 'Bhalo re Bhalo' : Sukumar Ray

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Soil Literacy Education Gets a Hands-On Makeover in Europe Reading Time: 3 minutes A European Union-funded initiative is expanding soil literacy education across 10 countries, helping students and citizens reconnect with the ground beneath their feet. Soil literacy education is taking root across Europe through a project called CURIOSOIL. The initiative teaches students, teachers, and everyday citizens why healthy soil matters. It launched in February 2024 and runs for four years, making it a long-term priority rather than a one-time campaign. CURIOSOIL is funded by the European Union and led by the University of Aveiro in Portugal. Fourteen partner organizations from 10 countries work together on the project. Their combined expertise spans natural science, education, and social science, giving the literacy education effort a wide research base to draw from. The project responds to a real gap. Many people never learn how soil supports food, water, and climate systems. CURIOSOIL calls this gap soil illiteracy and treats it as a barrier to protecting land for the future, which is exactly why soil literacy sits at the center of its mission. To close that gap, the team builds education tools for different age groups. These include curriculum materials for primary and secondary schools. Teachers also receive dedicated training programs so they can bring soil science into their own classrooms. The project also produces Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) for both higher education and primary and secondary teachers. It offers online challenges and micro-credential modules for university students. Guidelines for blended and remote learning round out the soil literacy education toolkit for educators who teach outside a traditional classroom. One tool is the Soil Curiosity Kit, a hands-on activity set for classrooms, gardens, and community spaces. Another is the World Soil Museum, an app that lets users explore soil types from their phone. A guiding character named Petra leads younger students through these lessons. CURIOSOIL also runs hackathons and art competitions called Artathons. These events invite students to reimagine soil health through design and technology. Winning ideas get shared across the project’s full partner network, extending the reach of soil literacy education beyond the schools that first tested it. This approach turns soil science into something creative rather than abstract. A student who builds an app about soil health understands the topic differently than one who only reads about it. That hands-on shift is central to how the project measures its success. CURIOSOIL extends soil literacy education beyond the textbook through hackathons and Artathons that challenge students to reimagine soil health through design and technology, with winning ideas shared across the project’s full 10-country network. Photo by Anna Shvets on Pexels. Beyond classrooms, CURIOSOIL works to influence policy. The team has already published a report analyzing soil education policies across Europe. It plans 15 additional national policy briefs, along with a final EU-wide brief containing recommendations for lawmakers on how to fund and scale the campaign. The project also built a Community of Practice, a network of educators and specialists who share soil teaching methods. Anyone working in soil education can join, whether they teach at a university or run a school garden program. The network exists so good ideas in soil literacy education spread, rather than staying isolated in one classroom or country. CURIOSOIL sits within the EU Mission Soil, a larger initiative to protect European soils by 2030. It coordinates with several sister projects tackling related soil health goals. Together, these efforts aim to reach farmers, students, and policymakers with consistent, science-based messaging. The scale of the challenge is worth noting. Europe has millions of students who could benefit from stronger soil literacy education, yet few schools currently teach the subject in depth. Closing even part of that gap could shift how an entire generation treats farmland, gardens, and green spaces. CURIOSOIL marked its latest milestone at the Soils for Europe Conference, held in Coimbra, Portugal, from September 7 to 11, 2026. The event brought together dozens of EU-funded soil projects to share results and plan next steps under the banner “Healthy Soils for a Sustainable Future,” with sessions spanning soil degradation, organic carbon stocks, biodiversity, and citizen engagement. The gathering reflected the project’s broader goal of connecting research with real classrooms, not just policy papers. Soil rarely gets the attention it deserves, despite holding the nutrients that grow the world’s food . Projects like CURIOSOIL are working to change that one lesson at a time. As more schools and communities invest in soil literacy education, that quiet resource under our feet may finally get the recognition it has always needed. The post Soil Literacy Education Gets a Hands-On Makeover in Europe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Liam Heneghan became a grandfather, he made a quiet promise: to be fully present in his granddaughter's life. Unlike his years as a busy father, when work and responsibilities often had pulled him away, he now devotes two full days each week to caring for his granddaughter, sharing in the ordinary rhythms of childhood. A Dublin-born ecologist, Heneghan finds himself rediscovering the natural world through her eyes -- from the wonder of a passing bird to the simple delight of exploring outdoors. Along the way, he's discovered that grandparenting offers something unexpected: a chance not only to give love, patience, and attention, but to receive the gift of seeing life anew. His story is a tender reminder that the most meaningful thing we can offer another person may be our time, freely and wholeheartedly given.

items.descriptionOriginal: By day, Vimal Kishore runs a small coffee stall in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. By night, he puts his earnings into something he has pursued for years: building machines that solve everyday problems. His latest creation is Lailo, a car he built for Rs 90,000 using parts from a scooter. Equipped with solar power, GPS and a rear-view camera, the vehicle grew out of his own need to travel independently. By running a coffee stall in Prayagraj, Vimal funds his experiments and turns everyday challenges into inventions. For Vimal, who lives with a disability affecting his legs, building a car was not just about creating a machine. It was about finding a way to drive despite the physical limitations that prevented him from using a conventional vehicle. When he decided to build his own car Vimal's journey began much earlier. When he was just eight months old, a severe fever affected his legs. Growing up, he watched other children walk, run and play, activities he could not participate in the same way. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) He eventually turned to understanding how things worked. Taking objects apart and putting them back together became a way to explore his curiosity and find better ways of doing things. In 2011, Vimal bought an Alto, hoping it would give him greater independence. However, his disability made it impossible for him to drive the car. Instead of giving up on the idea of travelling independently, he decided to build a vehicle of his own. Building a car without an engineering team Vimal began by drawing his design on paper and sourcing parts from discarded Ambassador cars. Working without a laboratory or a team of engineers, he put his ideas into practice with the resources available to him. The result was Lailo, a vehicle assembled using scooter parts and built at a cost of Rs 90,000. Its solar-powered system, GPS and rear-view camera add practical features to the design. Equipped with solar power, GPS and a rear-view camera, Lailo is Vimal's answer to a problem he faced himself. His coffee stall continues to fund his experiments. Every morning, he opens the counter to earn a living, while the money he saves goes towards researching and building new inventions. From scrap materials to miniature machines Lailo is only one part of Vimal's work. He has also made a power bank from scrap materials and a cooler using a discarded drum. Among his other creations is a working charkha measuring just 2.5 cm, which received recognition as a world record. His inventions have earned him wider recognition over the years, including an award from former President Dr APJ Abdul Kalam. Vimal's inventive spirit has earned him several accolades, including an award from former President Dr APJ Abdul Kalam. Despite these achievements, Vimal continues to run his coffee stall while pursuing his experiments. His work begins with problems he encounters in everyday life and the materials he can afford to access. Whether it is a vehicle that helps him travel independently or a machine assembled from discarded objects, he continues to find ways to turn limited resources into working solutions.
