items.descriptionOriginal: Under her courtroom table one day, Poonam Bamba found a red thread smeared with sindoor. Her peon, the court attendant who looks after the courtroom, urged her to wait. "Ma'am, please don't come to the dais yet," he said. "We are getting it cleaned, and only then should you come." A colleague once opened a case file and found cut hair inside it. The retired High Court judge says such moments belong to the part of judging that never reaches a judgment, and she keeps returning to them when she explains who sits on the bench. "People don't know that kind of pressure," she says. For Bamba, the point of these stories is simple. "Judges are not gods. They are as human as you and I are, and it is not easy to sit in that moment, listen to two people screaming at you and still maintain your calm," she tells The Better India. From the corporate world to the district bench Her own journey began far from a courtroom. In 2002, after a career in the corporate world, Bamba joined the district judiciary, the trial courts where most disputes first reach a judge . She took her oath quietly, before the district judge, in a ceremony she describes as far from pompous. From 125–150 cases a day to trials involving thousands of documents, Bamba describes the demanding realities of India's district courts. Photograph: ( Bar and Bench ) She was later elevated to the High Court , where the oath is a formal ceremony, but the quieter first one stayed with her. "I won't say that I made very big promises, but whenever I saw people appearing before me, there was always a desire that even if you help one person, your day is made," she says. A demanding routine That desire met a demanding routine almost at once. A judge's day begins with a cause list , the schedule of matters listed for hearing, and its length depends entirely on the court. Magistrates in her district handled 125 to 150 cases a day, against a pendency, or backlog of undecided cases, of 36,000, which she links largely to cheque-bouncing disputes. She corrects the common belief that every judge faces the same load. Additional sessions judges hear fewer matters, but murder trials keep them recording evidence from 10 am onwards. A judge in Canada or the US, she notes, may hear far fewer cases in a day. Her own courtroom later handled cases investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and terror-funding trials, where evidence recording ran continuously from 10 am to 4 pm. Some of those days ended without a single disposal, the term courts use for a case that has been decided and closed. Bamba credits stenographers, police officers and court staff, whose long hours and behind-the-scenes work keep the justice system running. Photograph: (AI-Generated image) "There are 10,000 documents in a case, and there are sometimes 20,000 documents in a case," she says. A full day of careful work, in other words, may not appear in the statistics at all. Bamba is quick to credit the people who share the room. Stenographers work the same hours as the judge, and even a short break means arranging for a colleague to take their seat. "Our stenographers are not able to move from their seats," she says. Police officers, she adds, sometimes work 36-hour shifts and are then deputed to give witness testimony straight after duty. In her view, they are as committed and as underappreciated as the judges they work alongside. Their effort sits within a national picture. Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told the Rajya Sabha on 23 July 2026 that 5.64 crore cases are pending across the Supreme Court, the 25 High Courts and the district and subordinate courts. National Judicial Data Grid figures as of 28 July, reported by Bar and Bench, show that 4.98 crore of those cases are in district and subordinate courts and 63.76 lakh are in the High Courts. NewsBytes reports that subordinate courts have 7,311 vacancies against a sanctioned strength of 30,868 judges. A judge answers to many people Bamba does not present the bench as a place beyond questions. The district judiciary, she says, follows the same conduct rules as IAS and IPS officers. "There is nothing different about us, as far as the district judiciary is concerned." Citizens unhappy with a district judge's conduct have a clear route. A complaint goes first to the district judge of that court, who can counsel the colleague informally or call them in separately. Lawyers can raise concerns in the same way. In one case, Bamba deputed a senior officer to sit quietly in a courtroom, observe a judge's conduct and report back. After more than two decades in the judiciary, Bamba urges young judges to approach the bench with humility, patience and empathy. Photograph: ( TNIE ) Typical complaints concern rudeness, sitting late or refusing urgent mentions, and she says citizens now notice. "Citizens are very alert these days," she says, and they increasingly record videos. Complaints with a vigilance angle, such as allegations of corruption or favouritism, go to the High Court. "The kind of scrutiny that happens in high courts, you cannot imagine," she says, adding that it reaches beyond a judge's conduct to individual judgments. She cites a sessions judge who granted bail, was criticised in the High Court for not knowing the law, and was then depicted in the Times of India in an AI-generated image walking to the Judicial Academy with a bag on his back. "What more scrutiny?" she asks. High Court and Supreme Court judges follow a different route, since the Constitution allows their removal only through impeachment. "The Constitution has already provided for that. Unless you amend the Constitution, what can we say?" she says. Scrutiny in the age of the screen Her strongest view concerns transparency. Bamba describes the judiciary as the most scrutinised institution in India. She believes audio-video recording and live streaming have opened proceedings to the public and invited more scrutiny than is warranted. "I feel we are very transparent, and still face ample scrutiny. Judges are not perfect, but they also function under umpteen pressures the public does not see. No one can be more accountable than a judge," she says. Her concern lies in how the recordings travel once they leave the courtroom. "Social media just pulls out one word that falls from your mouth and blows it up, and people react to the clip without reading the full judgment or order," she says. The same pressure, she says, changes how a judge behaves. "Even saying sorry will come out in the video, and then it will be published in full as if the judge misbehaved and then said sorry. It is stealing the natural way of being," she says. For citizens seeking justice, Bamba emphasises knowing their rights, asking lawyers for clarity and turning to free legal aid when they need support. Photograph: ( TNIE ) Technology has brought new demands as well. Video conferencing, introduced during Covid for remote appearances, is now sometimes misused. In her own court, a senior advocate appearing online said mid-hearing, "Excuse me, ma'am, my turn has come in the High Court," and vanished from the screen. "That was actually a serious misconduct. You just cannot run away from a district judge's court," she says. District judges have no contempt power of their own and must send a reference to the High Court, yet she chose another path. "I never believed in making references. I would rather decide a case at that time," she says. She doubts that artificial intelligence can ease the load in district courts yet. "AI can help you find similar judgments, but not this," she says, referring to the summarising of petitions. Most district courts still receive hard copies, while the Delhi High Court is fully digitised. What she tells young judges For young judges and lawyers, Bamba's advice begins with the self. "Power is given to us to dispense justice and not to flaunt," she says. "One's behaviour and attitude go a long way, so I would tell them to work on themselves first. When you can manage yourself, you can manage human resources, whether it is court staff, a litigant or a lawyer." Her method is practical, and she illustrates it with an example from her own bench. On several occasions, Bamba has spent hours, even days, studying evidence and preparing a judgment, only for one of the parties to seek an adjournment and delay the case further. "This has happened many times even though the case is more or less through. But instead of losing my cool, I learnt it is better to give a shorter date as requested. These are accommodations judges have to make all the time, despite packed schedules, workload and pressures," she says. She also trained herself to let provocation pass. "There have been times when lawyers or others have been rude to me and other judges. Lack of respect is very common and in these situations it is easy for any human to lose their temper. Over time, I trained myself to just ignore it as if I have not heard," she says. Whenever one gets angry, she adds, one should keep a little humility. In one such instance, a heated exchange ended and the day's cases were done, and she treated the matter as closed. The lawyer later apologised, and she considered it over. "They are not always bad or intentionally disrespectful. Empathy and placing ourselves in others' shoes is vital in this line of work," she says. What citizens can do Bamba believes citizens can ease the workload too, and she starts with the conversation between a litigant and a lawyer. "A citizen has every right to question their lawyer, ask for clarity, and push for a hearing date that feels realistic to them. Most of them are unaware of their own rights and some lawyers take advantage. Being aware as a citizen is important if they are visiting the court," she says. Understanding courts, however, takes effort, and Bamba admits it is hard to build. "Nobody wants to go to court," she says. Many people cannot afford to lose a day's wages to attend hearings, and even educated citizens and journalists tend to rely on media reports rather than reading the judgments themselves. The pressures that don't end there For judges, the strain does not stop at the courtroom door. Bamba recalls that in the days of typewriters, a single typing error could ruin an entire page and force the typist to start over. That pressure kept filings short and precise. Today, with copy and paste, lawyers can pad petitions to 100 or 200 pages with little effort. "We judges are also humans, and it takes us days to go through those files. But upon reading, we often realise that the same fact is stated in at least 20 ways, just to show the client that they have made such a comprehensive petition for them," she says. Unscrupulous lawyers, she adds, make the process harder for everyone. Some tell clients, "Give me Rs 50,000 and the matter will be decided in your favour," while the judge has no idea who is selling their name and judgment outside the courtroom. "Generally, unscrupulous lawyers play a very dirty role and judges bear the brunt," she says. Where to find help Bamba points to the services already in place. Legal services authorities run legal literacy campaigns and deploy paralegal volunteers to explain court procedures, though she says few people make use of them. The most direct help is free legal aid. "The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) runs a toll-free helpline on 15100 for those who qualify: women, children, members of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, persons in custody, and anyone whose annual income is below Rs 1,00,000 (or the limit notified by the Central or state government)," she explains. Applicants can submit an application on plain paper to the relevant legal services authority or fill in an e-form on the official portal. They can also visit legal aid clinics at courts and police stations, where legal aid lawyers and trained paralegal volunteers offer advice in person. A quieter kind of justice For Bamba, all of this returns to the people on both sides of the bench. Judges who work on themselves, litigants who plan realistically with their lawyers and citizens who know where to find help can make the process gentler for the stenographers, police and court staff who hold it together. The red thread under the table, the hair in the case file and the 20,000 documents in a single trial will never appear in a judgment or a statistic. They are the unseen weight of the job, and Bamba wants people to know it is carried by someone who is, in her own words, as human as everyone else in the room. It is the same belief she carried into that modest oath in 2002: that if she helps even one person, the day has been worthwhile.

items.title: Πώς οι χαρταετοί και το αρχαίο σχέδιο αντικαθιστούν τα καύσιμα στην εξερεύνηση της Ανταρκτικής
items.titleOriginal: How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Την τελευταία φορά που μια ομάδα ολοκλήρωσε μια παρόμοια διέλευση του εσωτερικού της Ανταρκτικής, έκαψε περίπου 170.000 λίτρα (περίπου 45.000 γαλόνια) καυσίμου για να το κάνει. Η αποστολή Wind Sled που έφυγε από την Ισπανία στις 18 Οκτωβρίου σχεδιάζει να μην χρησιμοποιήσει κανένα. Ο Ισπανός πολικός εξερευνητής Ramón Larramendi οδηγεί τέσσερα άτομα σε 3.400…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The last time a team completed a comparable crossing of Antarctica’s interior, they burned through roughly 170,000 liters (about 45,000 gallons) of fuel to do it. The Wind Sled expedition that left Spain on October 18 plans to use none. Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading four people across 3,400 kilometers (about 2,100 miles) of Antarctic interior on a kite-powered platform he has been designing for 25 years, with 16 research projects running the entire way. The vehicle runs on wind and solar energy , meaning no combustion engine at all. Twenty-five years of design, rooted in Inuit tradition Larramendi has spent 25 years developing the Wind Sled and has logged more than 28,000 kilometers (about 17,400 miles) across ice on earlier expeditions while refining it. The platform is built on Inuit sled-building techniques, which is an unusual starting point for a cutting-edge scientific research vehicle, and Larramendi doesn’t try to make it sound otherwise. “The wind sled is something completely unique in the world,” he says. “This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient.” The sled is 15 meters (about 49 feet) long across four modules, capable of carrying up to 2,100 kilograms (about 4,600 pounds). This expedition is running lighter, around 250 kilograms (about 550 pounds) of instruments. The crew has 20 kites ranging from five to 150 square meters (about 54 to 1,615 square feet) in sail area, swapped out as conditions change. The sled can hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour) in a strong wind; average cruising speed is around 25 (about 15 miles per hour). Sixteen research projects in terrain that rarely gets visited The route goes from Russia’s Novolazarevskaya base in Queen Maud Land, through the Pole of Inaccessibility and near the Pole of Cold, finishing at the Concordia research station at Dome C. Five scientific stations will be established along the way. The 16 projects were selected by Spain’s polar research committee, with collaborators including NASA’s Ames Research Center , six Spanish universities, and several national research bodies. One of the NASA projects is asking whether salt rocks sitting on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. Sensors embedded in the rocks will measure temperature, humidity, and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water could form inside them despite conditions that make that seem impossible. It’s the kind of question that sounds like astrobiology because it basically is. The Dinglac project will use ground-penetrating radar to map the top 10 meters (about 33 feet) of snow to track how ice layers accumulate and shift. The campaign will also sample for microplastics and chemical pollutants, test for microorganisms and viruses, and run assessments of the European Galileo navigation system . The location makes all of it harder to get any other way. Satellites and permanent stations have limited reach into this interior. “It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data,” Larramendi says. The crew are their own experiment All four team members are Antarctic veterans: Larramendi; Hilo Moreno , a polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki , a researcher at the University of Maine; and Javier Selva , a documentary filmmaker who crossed Antarctica with Larramendi in 2011-2012. They’re also research subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre of the University of Cádiz, will monitor the team’s psychological responses, sleep, and social dynamics across the 85 days. The data is meant to inform planning for long-duration space missions, where small crews face confinement and extreme isolation from Earth, conditions the interior of Antarctica replicates about as well as anywhere. “We are the experiment ourselves,” Larramendi says. “Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent.” A route designed to be repeated The point isn’t just to complete this crossing. Each return trip lets researchers compare data across seasons to track real changes in ice, climate, and polar ecosystems over time. “Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations,” Larramendi says. When the team arrives at Concordia, they’ll fly out and leave the sled dismantled at the station, ready for the return journey. The fuel comparison says most of what needs saying: the last comparable crossing burned through about 45,000 gallons. This one runs on kites and a design that’s been in development since the 1990s, and when it’s done, the plan is to come back. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You’re doing everything right at bedtime: you stay away from screens after nine, take a soothing dark shower , sip on that herbal tea cooling on the nightstand, and maintain a reasonably consistent sleep schedule. Yet some nights the ceiling still has your full attention past midnight, and you can’t quite figure out why. If you’ve been treating sleep as mostly a habits problem, a recent nutritional review suggests there’s a variable you might be overlooking: what you eat in the evening. The review, published in the journal Nutrients , made the case for pistachios as a bedtime snack, and the reasoning holds up better than most food-and-sleep claims do. There’s no single magic compound, but what’s unusual is that one ounce of pistachios stacks five separate sleep-relevant nutrients at once, each arriving via a different route. That’s a rare combination to find in a single snack. Why diet is an underused sleep lever Most sleep advice focuses on behavior such as consistent wake times, a cool and dark room, or no caffeine past the early afternoon. Diet gets surprisingly little attention, even though a lot of research connects eating patterns to how well people sleep. People who follow the Mediterranean or DASH diets tend to sleep better, and both lean on nuts and legumes. That link pushed researchers to look more closely at which nutrients might be responsible. With pistachios, there turned out to be several working at the same time. Vitamin B6, tryptophan, and the sleep hormone chain One ounce of pistachios provides close to 40 percent of your daily vitamin B6, more than any other tree nut. This is noteworthy because B6 is what your body uses to turn tryptophan into serotonin, and serotonin is the raw material for melatonin. B6 also helps produce GABA, the neurotransmitter that tells your nervous system to settle down at night. The same one-ounce serving contains about 71 milligrams of tryptophan. In a survey of more than 11,000 Spanish university students, higher tryptophan intake was tied to longer sleep and a lower likelihood of insomnia. In a separate trial , adults between 55 and 75 who ate tryptophan-enriched cereal for a week fell asleep faster, slept longer, and produced more melatonin than those eating standard cereal. Plant-made melatonin, found in the nut itself Plants make their own melatonin, called phytomelatonin, and it has nothing to do with the melatonin your body makes from tryptophan. One analysis of American pistachios found roughly 18.7 micrograms per serving, which puts them in the same range as tart cherry and tomato, two foods with a reasonable body of sleep research behind them. Other analyses have found lower amounts, so the exact number varies, but phytomelatonin shows up in pistachios consistently. Magnesium, fiber, and the gut Magnesium supports melatonin production and plays a role in deep sleep through GABA activity. Pistachios have about 31 milligrams per ounce, around 10 percent of the recommended daily amount. Almonds have more (76 milligrams in the same serving), but every bit adds up. The CARDIA study , which tracked a large group of young adults over many years, found that those with the highest magnesium intake slept better and were less likely to get fewer than seven hours a night. A one-ounce serving of pistachios also covers about 11 percent of your daily fiber. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, which have been linked to sleep quality. In a lab comparison of common nuts, pistachios produced the most of these compounds. They also rank second among tree nuts in polyphenols, and a recent meta-analysis found polyphenol supplements helped people with sleep disorders fall asleep faster and sleep longer, though most of those trials used extracts rather than whole foods. The clinical trials that haven’t happened yet No study has directly tested whether eating pistachios helps people sleep better. The review draws a reasonable line through a lot of supporting research, but connecting individual nutrient mechanisms to actual sleep outcomes still requires human trials that don’t exist yet. It’s also important to note that the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers . If you already snack in the evening, a small handful of pistachios, around 28 grams, is an easy substitution to run for a week. The usual sleep hygiene advice still stands, and matters more than any snack. But if you’ve already worked through that list and you’re still not sleeping well, what you eat before bed is a reasonable next thing to look at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Ερευνητές στο Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) και στο College of Education and Human Development διαπίστωσαν ότι τα αυξανόμενα επίπεδα δύο microRNAs, kn…
items.descriptionOriginal: Pancreatic cancer cells are remarkably good at growing, but new research suggests that two tiny molecules already present in the body may help slow them down. Researchers at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) and the College of Education and Human Development found that increasing levels of two microRNAs, known as miR-15a and miR-16, reduced protein synthesis and slowed the growth of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells. In a study in Physiological Reports , the researchers also shared that patients with higher levels of the microRNAs in their tumors tended to live longer, further supporting their potential as targets for new pancreatic cancer treatments. “Cancer cells continually proliferate, or grow and divide,” says James Fluckey, associate dean for research and a professor in the kinesiology and sport management department and the study’s principal investigator. “To do that, the cells need to increase processes like protein synthesis that give them what they need to grow. If you disrupt that protein synthesis, you can slow the rate at which those cells can grow.” MicroRNAs are short strands of genetic material that help regulate which proteins a cell produces. Rather than providing instructions for making proteins themselves, they can bind to genetic messages and prevent those instructions from being translated into proteins. That gives microRNAs considerable influence over what happens inside a cell. Peter Nghiem, an associate professor in the VMBS veterinary integrative biosciences department, compared their role to the brakes on a car. “Their expression can prevent something very bad from happening—like accelerating to the point where you crash or develop cancer,” he says. When levels of miR-15a and miR-16 are reduced, as the researchers observed in pancreatic cancer, that braking effect may be diminished, so the team explored what happens when those microRNAs are added back. “The whole goal with this study was not to repair the brakes but bring the brakes back into the cell to see if we can slow down the progression of these cancer types,” Fluckey says. To test that idea, the researchers increased miR-15a and miR-16 in cultured PDAC cells. Doing so reduced both protein synthesis and cell proliferation. The study builds on the team’s previous research into miR-15a and miR-16 by examining how the two microRNAs influence protein production and cell growth in pancreatic cancer. The team also used computational analysis to identify the biological processes potentially influenced by the two microRNAs, revealing connections to a broad range of genes and pathways involved in cancer, protein metabolism, cell adhesion and other cellular processes. That broad influence could be particularly important because cancer is rarely driven by a single malfunctioning process. “We would love to find that magic bullet to say, ‘This is the molecule that causes cancer,’ but we can’t,” Fluckey says. “What we can say is that these microRNAs seem to have a vital role in the protein balance of the cell. When they are in abundance, we can dramatically slow the progression of that cancer.” The researchers next turned to publicly available patient data to determine whether the patterns they observed in cultured cells were also reflected in people with pancreatic disease. They found that miR-15a and miR-16 levels were lower in pancreatic tumors than in healthy pancreatic tissue. They also found that microRNAs were also reduced in samples from patients with pancreatitis, an inflammatory condition of the pancreas. Most notably, pancreatic cancer patients whose tumors had higher miR-15a and miR-16 expression had better survival outcomes than those with lower expression. Together, the patient data reinforced the researchers’ laboratory findings, showing that the same microRNAs that slowed cancer cell growth in cultured cells were also associated with better outcomes in people with pancreatic cancer. While the results point toward therapeutic possibilities, turning miR-15a and miR-16 into a treatment will require solving a major challenge: getting them to the right cells. The researchers’ next goal is to develop a delivery method capable of restoring the microRNAs specifically in cancer cells while leaving healthy cells alone. “We’re becoming more and more confident that the miR-15a and 16 interventions may truly have therapeutic potential,” Fluckey says. “Now we just have to figure out how to get it to cells in a way that we’re only treating the cells that are cancerous.” That specificity will be critical, Nghiem says, because microRNAs also perform important regulatory functions in healthy cells. The researchers also caution that restoring miR-15a and miR-16 is unlikely to become a stand-alone cure for pancreatic cancer; instead, it could eventually provide one component of a combination of treatments targeting the many biological processes involved in the disease. “It’s just not going to be one treatment for a disease,” Nghiem says. “MicroRNA-15a and 16 can be one important arm of a treatment regimen. As we do research, we’re going to find all of the pieces that come together eventually to effectively treat and hopefully cure patients with these devastating diseases.” For Fluckey, one of the most promising aspects of the research is that those potential tools already exist naturally within the body. “The therapeutic intervention that we’re looking at is already in your body,” he says. “We just have to figure out how to get it back in working order.” Source: Texas A&M University The post 2 molecules may help slow pancreatic cancer growth appeared first on Futurity .

What may look like simple patterns carries a deeper meaning. In a city where many young people have moved away and elderly parents may be left feeling alone, her colourful artwork brings unexpected joy to people’s mornings. Inspired by generations of Bengali artistic tradition, Ratnabali is doing more than decorating doorsteps. She’s helping keep a fading cultural art form alive while reminding people that even a small gesture can make someone feel noticed and valued. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Creating a More Sustainable Workplace Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Sustainability has moved from being a nice extra to something many businesses are expected to think about as part of everyday operations. Customers, employees and clients are increasingly interested in how organisations manage energy, waste and travel, but creating a greener workplace doesn’t necessarily require a dramatic redesign or a huge environmental budget. The good news is that creating a greener workplace does not always require major investment. Often, the most effective changes are simple adjustments that reduce environmental impact while improving day-to-day operations. The workspace itself can play a big part. For some businesses, this could mean looking at how they use their office space, while others are reducing unnecessary travel and allowing their staff to work from home and only meeting face-to-face for genuine reasons. Those trying to reduce travel emissions find that some cities offer flexible office space, like Leeds . These coworking and flexible office options can reduce the need for employees to travel into a permanent office every day when face-to-face collaboration is only required occasionally. Businesses that require regular in-person collaboration are increasingly choosing locations with strong public transport connections. This can help reduce reliance on car travel and make lower-carbon commuting a practical choice for more employees. Make Energy Efficiency an Everyday Habit Energy efficiency sounds like a major infrastructure project, but plenty of improvements begin with ordinary workplace habits. Lights left on in empty meeting rooms, computers running overnight and heating operating when nobody is in the building all represent avoidable energy use. Reducing energy use can lower operating costs while also helping organisations cut the emissions associated with powering their workplace. Motion-sensitive lighting, sensible heating controls and making sure equipment is switched off when it isn’t required can make an immediate difference. Businesses can also look at practical ways to reduce workplace energy consumption , including reviewing heating schedules, monitoring usage and considering smarter controls. Make Greener Commuting Easier Supporting cycling, walking and public transport can be as simple as providing secure bike storage, showers or clearer information about nearby transport connections. Flexible and hybrid working can help too. Fewer commuting journeys can also help lower transport-related carbon emissions, making hybrid working beneficial for both employees and the environment. If employees don’t need to be physically present every day, reducing unnecessary journeys may be more practical than expecting everyone to commute simply because that’s how the working week has traditionally been structured. The key is making greener choices convenient. People are far more likely to change their habits when the alternative actually works for their lives. Reduce Waste Without Making Work More Complicated Sustainability initiatives tend to lose momentum when they create additional hassle. Waste reduction works best when the greener option is also the easiest one. Moving routine documents online can reduce unnecessary printing, while clearly labelled recycling points make it easier for employees to dispose of things correctly. Reviewing purchasing habits can help as well. Ordering fewer disposable supplies, reusing equipment where possible and resisting the temptation to replace perfectly serviceable office furniture all add up. Get the Team Involved Finally, no workplace sustainability plan will get very far if it exists only in a policy document nobody reads. Employees need to understand what the organisation is trying to achieve and, ideally, feel that they have some ownership of it. That might mean creating small team targets, inviting staff to suggest improvements or simply making recycling, energy saving and sustainable travel part of everyday workplace conversations. Progress doesn’t need to be turned into a competition, but sharing the results can help people see that individual actions genuinely add up. Over time, small changes to energy use, commuting habits and waste management can reduce a workplace’s environmental impact while supporting wider sustainability goals. The post Creating a More Sustainable Workplace appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals Reading Time: 2 minutes Businesses across the UK are facing more and more pressure to reduce their environmental impact while maintaining operational efficiency. Both customers and investors are paying closer attention to sustainability commitments, and many organisations are being encouraged to look for practical ways to make a real impact with long-term environmental goals. While most initiatives often focus on transport , energy use and supply chains, technology decisions also play an important role. Many organisations are now reviewing how their IT infrastructure contributes to their wider sustainability strategy. By adopting scalable digital solutions and working with providers that offer Managed Cloud services for improved efficiency and resource management , businesses can reduce unnecessary energy consumption while maintaining the performance and flexibility needed to support growth. Reducing reliance on energy-intensive on-site infrastructure Traditional on-site IT infrastructure can require significant resources to operate and maintain. Physical servers consume electricity around the clock and often require dedicated cooling systems to prevent overheating. As equipment ages, performance can decline, leading to increased maintenance demands and higher operating costs. Moving workloads into efficiently managed cloud environments can help reduce the energy demands associated with maintaining multiple on-site servers. For example, your business may replace ageing server equipment with cloud-hosted applications and storage solutions rather than investing in additional physical infrastructure. Supporting flexible and remote working Cloud technology has transformed the way employees access business systems and collaborate with colleagues. Staff can securely access files and data from different locations, whether they are working from home or visiting client sites. This flexibility can support your objectives by reducing the need for daily commuting and frequent business travel. For example, team members can collaborate on projects remotely using cloud-based platforms. Alongside environmental benefits, flexible access can improve employee satisfaction and help organisations attract and retain talent. Businesses that support remote working and secure access to business systems can often create a more agile, environmentally friendly operating model. Making better use of business resources Another advantage of cloud technology is scalability. Unlike traditional infrastructure , businesses do not need to purchase large amounts of hardware in anticipation of future demand. Instead, you can increase or decrease capacity as requirements change. For example, a retailer may temporarily increase storage or computing resources during a busy trading period without investing in additional physical equipment that may sit unused for much of the year. This approach helps reduce waste and prevents overinvestment. Improving monitoring and reporting Accurate data is essential for sustainability targets. Cloud-based platforms often provide advanced reporting and monitoring capabilities that can help you gain better visibility into your operations. You could use cloud-based dashboards to analyse performance metrics and identify inefficiencies across different departments or locations. This information can support more informed decision-making and help businesses prioritise areas for improvement. Better access to data can also assist with reporting, making it easier to measure progress against environmental goals and demonstrate accountability to stakeholders. To summarise… While sustainability requires a broad business commitment, being fully sustainable for many businesses is not something that can be achieved quickly. Cloud adoption can be an important step towards reducing resource consumption, improving operational efficiency and supporting long-term environmental goals. The post How Cloud Technology Can Support Business Sustainability Goals appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim Reading Time: 3 minutes Examples of Medical Errors That May Lead to a Malpractice Claim According to a study published in Patient Safety and highlighted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), diagnostic errors accounted for 26.6% of closed medical malpractice claims reviewed over a 20-year period. Among all claims related to the diagnoses, 39% were fatal. Misdiagnosis and delay in diagnoses were the most often made claims. Medical malpractices have severe implications for patients, which may range from delays in treatment to deterioration of medical conditions or even disability and death. In the USA, one is entitled to filing medical malpractice if a healthcare professional fails to adhere to the acceptable level of care, resulting in preventable harm. There are actually more malpractice cases that happen in the healthcare industry than people realize. But it’s also important to understand that not all unfavorable medical outcomes qualify as malpractice. A claim will require evidence of negligence and resulting injury. But what is an example of malpractice ? Let’s take a closer look at the common medical errors and what steps you need to take to seek a possible claim. Diagnosis Is Where Most of It Happens In the AHRQ systematic review of ED care, the rate of diagnostic errors was found to be 5.7% with an extrapolated estimate of 7.4 million diagnostic errors and 371,000 severe harms per year associated with diagnostic errors. These overall rates were based on results from three prospective studies conducted outside of the U.S. in Canada, Spain, and Switzerland. AHRQ commissioned an independent review after its publication because of the high numbers that were cited. This is an order of magnitude, not a number count. Rates of disease-specific errors have higher validity. On average, physicians fail to diagnose stroke in about 17% of patients. The list is completed by myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, spinal cord compression, and venous thromboembolism. These conditions share a profile. They present atypically often enough that a physician working quickly can reach the wrong conclusion. The Procedure Itself Surgical and anesthesia errors sit at the opposite end of the evidentiary range. Wrong-site surgery. A retained sponge. An anesthesia dosing failure during a routine case. Proof of breach in wrong-site and retained object surgeries is seldom disputed since there is evidence of negligence in the records. Firms handling this work tend to sort it by mechanism rather than by specialty. Medical malpractice lawyers in Marietta, GA , separate birth injuries such as cerebral palsy, brachial plexus injury, and hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy from anesthesia errors, emergency room errors, and surgical errors. Medication Errors More defendants get implicated in medication cases than any other type. A prescriber orders a prescription, a pharmacist dispenses the prescription, a nurse delivers the prescription, and the electronic health record alerts for a possible drug interaction or not. Wrong dosage, lack of allergy information, and drugs with similar appearances on the screen cause claims. Each individual has his own employer and his own insurance. Birth Injuries Obstetric negligence claims hinge more on timing than anything else. Whether or not someone interpreted the fetal monitoring properly. How quickly the decision was made to utilize the C-section procedure. Whether or not the procedures used were appropriate for shoulder dystocia. These cases require more time than adult claims. In fact, some states also set a separate limitations period for minors in malpractice cases that ends well before adulthood. What Turns an Error Into a Claim Expert testimony does most of the work. A plaintiff cannot establish the standard of care without a qualified physician stating what it was. A number of states, including Georgia, require a sworn expert affidavit filed alongside the complaint. That single requirement can end a case before anyone takes a deposition. Damage caps are the other structural variable. It’s important to understand, though, that these caps could shift. The non-economic damage cap in California remained unchanged at $250,000 for decades before AB 35 changed it to $350,000 for cases other than death. It is at $500,000 for wrongful death starting from 2023, increasing by $40,000 and $50,000, respectively, each year for ten years. The distance between a medical error and a malpractice claim is mostly documentary. Whether the chart recorded the symptom the patient actually reported. Whether the monitoring strip survived. Whether anybody wrote down a time. Errors are common and claims are not, and most of what fills the space between those two facts is records that either exist or do not. items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells.

items.descriptionOriginal: October is a good time to grow spinach on your terrace in many parts of India, as temperatures begin to ease after the summer heat. With a few containers, suitable soil, and regular care, even a small terrace can provide fresh palak for everyday meals. The key is to give the plants enough light, maintain moisture in the soil, and choose growing conditions suited to the season. Vijay Sharma, a swimming coach at SP College in Bikaner , Rajasthan, knows the satisfaction of harvesting vegetables at home. He began gardening in 2017 after noticing that the quality of market-bought cluster beans was declining. Pleased with the results, he started growing spinach, okra, chillies, and other vegetables. During the COVID-19 lockdown, he expanded his garden to cover 1,500 square feet, growing more than 150 varieties of vegetables and medicinal plants. In a conversation with The Better Indi a published in October 2021, he shared how he prepared his growing medium, reused household materials as planters, and cared for his plants. His experience offers useful lessons for those planning to grow spinach this October. 1. Choose a suitable container Spinach grows well in containers, making it a practical choice for terrace gardeners. Choose a pot or grow bag at least six to eight inches deep, with drainage holes to prevent water from collecting around the roots. A wider container allows you to grow several plants together. October is a good time to grow spinach on your terrace in many parts of India. Photograph: (The Arbor Gate) The expert found creative ways to expand his garden when gardening supplies were difficult to access during the lockdown. He reused discarded drums, old tyres, and broken plastic containers as planters. For spinach, use a clean container that allows excess water to drain freely. Avoid overcrowding the plants, as adequate space helps leaves develop well. 2. Prepare a nutrient-rich growing medium Healthy leaves begin with good soil. Spinach needs a growing medium that retains moisture without becoming waterlogged. Sharma explains that he uses soil mixed with cow dung manure or cocopeat, with these materials accounting for around half of his growing mix. For spinach, combine garden soil with well-rotted compost and cocopeat to create a loose, moisture-retentive medium. Use mature compost rather than fresh manure, which can damage plants and is unsuitable for direct application to leafy vegetables. 3. Sow seeds directly into the pot Spinach seeds can be sown directly into the container where the plants will grow. Place them in shallow furrows, cover lightly with soil, and water gently. Keep the soil moist while the seeds germinate. Once seedlings appear, thin them out if they are growing too close together. This gives the remaining plants room to develop healthy leaves. October is suitable for sowing spinach in many parts of India, particularly northern regions where temperatures begin to fall. In warmer areas, choose a cooler spot on the terrace and avoid exposing seedlings to excessive afternoon heat. 4. Give spinach adequate sunlight Spinach needs sufficient sunlight for healthy growth, but intense heat can cause it to struggle. Choose a spot that receives several hours of sunlight, preferably in the morning if your terrace becomes very hot later in the day. The gardener has observed how vegetation can influence temperatures in his garden. He explains that creepers shelter his plants from direct sunlight and help cool the garden during summers when temperatures in Bikaner can approach 50 degrees Celsius. For spinach, aim for a balance. Avoid deep shade, but provide some protection from harsh afternoon sun in warmer regions. 5. Water regularly without soaking the soil Spinach needs consistent moisture, especially during germination and early growth . Dry soil can affect leaf development, while excess water can damage the roots. Spinach grows well in containers, making it a practical choice for terrace gardeners. Photograph: (Nature & Garden) Sharma advises beginners to pay attention to watering. "Watering the plants is equally important for their healthy growth," he says. Check the soil regularly and water when the surface begins to dry. Water gently around the base of the plants, allowing excess moisture to drain through the container. Pots exposed to strong sunlight or dry winds may need more frequent checks. 6. Feed the plants and keep an eye on their leaves A growing medium enriched with compost gives spinach a good start. If the plants remain in the same container for several weeks, add a light layer of mature compost around them to replenish nutrients. Inspect the leaves regularly for holes, discolouration, or pests. Remove damaged leaves and avoid overcrowding, which can restrict airflow. The gardener advises beginners to grow seasonal vegetables and says that plants need occasional trimming. For spinach, remove damaged foliage while leaving healthy leaves and the central growing point intact. 7. Harvest without uprooting the plant Once the outer leaves are large enough to use, harvest them carefully while leaving the central growing point undisturbed. This allows the plant to continue producing leaves. The first harvest may be ready in around four to six weeks , depending on the variety, temperature, and growing conditions. For a more regular supply, sow small batches of seeds at intervals rather than planting everything at once. For spinach, use a clean container that allows excess water to drain freely. Photograph: (Gardener's Path) Sharma's terrace garden shows how growing vegetables at home can begin with a simple experiment and expand over time. For beginners, a couple of spinach containers are a good starting point. TBI Gardening Calendar brings together what to plant, grow, and care for each month of the year, helping home gardeners make the most of their balconies, terraces, backyards, and small growing spaces. Each story focuses on seasonal plants and crops, with simple, practical guidance on when to sow or plant, how to care for them, and what to expect as they grow.

items.description: Πρώτον, τα καλά νέα: Ο κόσμος μπορεί να είναι πολύ πιο κοντά από ό,τι πιστεύουμε σε έναν διεθνή στόχο προστασίας του 30% της γης έως το 2030. Τα κακά νέα: Μάλλον δεν είναι η σωστή γη. Τα έθνη του κόσμου έχουν θέσει προστασία στο 27% περίπου των χερσαίων μαζών του πλανήτη, πολύ περισσότερο από το 19% που πιστευόταν προηγουμένως, σύμφωνα με έρευνα που δημοσιεύθηκε πρόσφατα…
items.descriptionOriginal: First, the good news: The world might be a lot closer than we think to an international goal of protecting 30% of land by 2030. The bad news: It’s probably not all the right land. The nations of the world have placed protections on roughly 27% of the planet’s land masses, far more than the 19% previously thought, according to research recently published in Nature . There has been much hand wringing among conservation-minded folks that countries were woefully behind on land protection pledges made in 2022 to shield 30% of Earth’s land and 30% of the ocean from development as part of an update to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the main international agreement aimed at the current extinction crisis. But “our analysis suggests that much more of the land is in some type of conservation area than currently recognized,” said lead author Helen O’Neill, a postdoctoral researcher at the United Kingdom’s Institute of Zoology, London. The official tally tracking protected lands is a database at the Protected Planet website , a collaboration between the United Nations and the International Union for Conservation of Nature. While this is the authoritative source, it’s incomplete. Some protected land hasn’t been registered there by countries. And it doesn’t include significant acreage that falls into a kind of gray area – land that isn’t formally protected chiefly for wildlife, but where regulations provide many of the same benefits. Known as “other effective area-based conservation measures” or OECMs, this might include land protected as sacred by Indigenous groups or managed to improve water quality. O’Neill and 35 other scientists from across the globe set out to tally this overlooked land to create a more complete picture. To reduce the massive effort required to scrutinize the status of every piece of land on the planet, the researcher selected pieces totaling 10% of all the world’s land masses. That included terrain scattered across the world and covering major types of ecosystems, from the Rocky Mountains in Montana to the Amazonian jungle to the desert of the Arabian Peninsula. .IRPP_ruby where regulations and management practices made them good candidates for being OECMs. The scientists used the results to create a computer model that estimated how this pattern would apply to the entire world. The result was the encouraging estimate that 26.8% of all land is protected, at least on paper. But that doesn’t mean conservationists can cruise across the 2030 finish line with their arms raised. Because the research also revealed troubling holes in where these lands are being conserved. Of the 173 different ecological regions scientists have mapped around the world, fewer than 100 have greater than 17% of their land protected, the scientists estimated. Regions that are primarily ice and rock – polar and alpine landscapes – are significantly overrepresented in the catalog of protected areas. That’s not a big surprise, since those regions are often less attractive for human settlement or exploitation by farming or other activities. By contrast, deserts, woodlands, grasslands and temperate forests all fall below the 30% target. Then there is the question of whether land that’s conserved on paper is really being protected . The new research points to the potential gains that can be made, particularly with the recognition of the conservation potential of these OECMs. But “conserving 30% of land and seas is not sufficient on its own,” said Heather Bingham, a co-author who heads the Protected Planet Initiative. “The target also calls for these areas to be managed effectively for positive biodiversity outcomes, and to be placed where they will have the greatest impact on biodiversity.” O’Neill, et. al. “ Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates .” Nature. items.title: «Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In»: Αυτά τα είδωλα Durga των καλλιτεχνών της Καλκούτα δεν θα πνίξουν το Hooghly This Pujo
items.titleOriginal: ‘Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In’: These Kolkata Artisans’ Durga Idols Won’t Choke the Hooghly This Pujo
items.description: Στο Joy Durga Bhandar, ένα εργαστήριο στο Kumartuli της βόρειας Καλκούτα, ο Koushik Ghosh ξεκινά ένα είδωλο με ένα πλαίσιο από μπαμπού και ξύλο δεμένο μεταξύ τους με σχοινί από γιούτα. Από αυτή τη βάση προέρχονται οι γλυπτές φιγούρες, οι διακοσμήσεις και τα στρώματα χρώματος που βλέπουν οι θιασώτες κατά τη διάρκεια της Durga Puja. Ο Koushik ξέρει καλά αυτή τη διαδικασία. Για γενιές, οι τεχνίτες στο Kumartuli φορούσαν…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Joy Durga Bhandar, a workshop in north Kolkata's Kumartuli, Koushik Ghosh begins an idol with a framework of bamboo and wood tied together with jute rope. From this base come the sculpted figures, decorations and layers of colour that devotees see during Durga Puja. Koushik knows this process well. For generations, artisans in Kumartuli have worked with bamboo, straw and clay, shaping idols by hand for Kolkata's Durga Puja celebrations. Over time, many workshops also adopted thermocol decorations, synthetic paints and plastic ornaments because they were quicker or cheaper to use. Koushik is looking for ways to bring more traditional materials back into his work. "The frame, the clay, the straw, those were always ours. The thermocol and the chemical colours came later, because they were cheaper and faster. I am going back to what was here before," he says. The straw framework gives the idol its shape before artisans add the first layers of clay. He is working towards idols decorated with natural clay, shola (the soft pith of a plant used for delicate ornaments) and natural colours instead of thermocol. Every year, after Durga Puja, thousands of idols are immersed in the Hooghly River and other water bodies. In 2025, around 5,200 idols were immersed across 34 major Hooghly ghats and approximately 30 other water bodies in Kolkata and nearby suburbs, according to The Times of India . Civic workers clear debris from immersion sites, but thermocol and plastic decorations need careful collection and disposal because they can persist in the environment. Neel, a volunteer who has spent several seasons cleaning the Hooghly's banks near Babughat, remembers finding thermocol floating on the surface, coloured residue near the banks, and plastic decorations gathering along the ghats. Kumartuli's workshops have produced clay idols for Kolkata's Durga Puja for generations. For Koushik, the challenge is to make the decorations less wasteful while keeping the craft affordable for the families who depend on it. From bamboo frames to Durga's eyes: Inside the craft of Kumartuli Walking through Kumartuli's narrow lanes, the smell of wet clay is difficult to miss. The neighbourhood, whose name comes from kumor (potter) and tuli (neighbourhood quarter), has been home to idol makers for more than three centuries. Its workshops stand between Rabindra Sarani and the Hooghly, the river that has long supplied the fine alluvial soil used in their craft. Traditionally known as Ganga maati , this clay is softer and finer than ordinary earth, allowing artisans to sculpt delicate features. Artisans shape clay over the bamboo-and-straw framework before adding finer details and colour. At Koushik's workshop, everything begins with the kathamo (a framework made from bamboo and wood). "The frame is not just engineering," he explains. "It is the first thing she stands on." The structure must support the central Durga figure, accompanying figures, a lion and other sculpted elements. Next comes khar bandha (tying straw around the frame). Carefully shaped bundles of straw form the arms, waist, chest and other features. If the straw is tied incorrectly, the figure may lose its balance or the clay may crack. The first clay layer is entel mati (sticky clay mixed with tush , or rice husk). It takes about three to four days to dry. Straw and clay form the idol's limbs, which must be balanced before the finer layers are applied. Artisans then apply bele mati (finer, smoother clay), allowing another five or six days for drying, depending on the weather. Any cracks are repaired with fresh mud. Faces, hands and other delicate parts are often made separately using chhach (moulds), helping workshops manage the large number of orders they receive. The final detailing includes chokkhudaan (painting the eyes). Some artisans specialise in this stage because even a slight difference in the brushstrokes can change the expression of the figure. This process has remained largely familiar across generations. A Durga idol includes accompanying figures and a lion, all assembled before the final decoration. The changes have come in the materials used for decoration and finishing. Earlier, artisans relied on bamboo, straw, jute, shola and natural pigments. Tamarind-seed gum, chalk powder and starch made from boiled arrowroot were used to prepare and finish colours. As demand grew, thermocol became popular for chaal (decorative backdrops), mukut (crowns) and ornaments. Synthetic paints offered brighter colours, while plastic jewellery entered some workshops. These alternatives were quicker, cheaper and easier to work with when deadlines were approaching. The extra work behind a natural finish Gopal, a veteran artisan who remembers making idols before thermocol became common, understands why workshops adopted it. He recalls decorating traditional sabeki pratima (traditional-style idols) with shola, cloth, zari and daaker saaj (traditional decorative work). Handmade clay figures require repeated shaping and drying, adding to an artisan's working hours. "Shola was beautiful, but it took time. Thermocol came because it was fast and cheap. If you remove thermocol now and don't give me shola at the same price and within the same time, I am just working slower for the same money," he says. Thermocol is lightweight, easy to cut and relatively inexpensive. Shola, jute, handmade paper, paper pulp, bamboo and clay ornaments may require more time and skill, and sometimes cost more. Natural colours create another difficulty. Asha, who manages colouring and finishing work at a Kumartuli studio, says buyers have grown accustomed to the bright, uniform finish of synthetic paints. "Natural colour is more beautiful if you know how to look at it. But the buyer is standing under LED lights in the pandal. They want brightness. Softness looks like less work to them, even when it is more," she explains. Colouring and decoration come after sculpting, with buyers often expecting a bright, even finish. This expectation has financial consequences. Koushik points to raw-material prices, labour, drying time and the risk of damage as factors that can raise the cost of working with natural materials. Handmade decorations take more hours. Natural colours need careful application. During the monsoon, wet clay can also take longer to dry. In the final weeks of a season, artisans often work long hours to meet delivery dates, using fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions. Koushik has not lost an idol to rain, but the possibility remains with every order that needs additional drying time. Artisans use fans and tarpaulins to manage damp conditions while working to Puja deadlines. The bigger challenge is recovering these expenses. There is no fixed price for a Durga idol. The cost depends on its height, design, decorations, arrangement of figures and the buyer's budget. Even two idols of the same height can have different prices. Costs differ by design, materials and year, so there is no single price difference between idols using natural decorations and those made with synthetic alternatives. For a small workshop, even a modest unplanned expense can make a difference. "If the idol has to be eco-friendly and the client wants the same finish as a synthetic-painted one, one of us has to absorb the difference. Usually, it is us," Asha says. The cost of an idol depends on its size, design, decorative materials and time spent finishing it. A South Kolkata Puja committee organiser, who requested anonymity, describes the buyer's dilemma. His committee relies on contributions from neighbourhood families, so any increase in an idol's price or change in its appearance must be discussed with the people paying for it. Gopal believes buyers and artisans should agree on materials and costs when placing an order. That would help workshops plan their purchases without bearing unexpected expenses themselves. After the idols are immersed, what is left in the Hooghly? Idol immersion is an important part of Durga Puja. The environmental concern lies with synthetic decorations and paints that may enter the water or be left on the banks unless they are removed and collected. Thermocol and plastic do not biodegrade easily and can break into smaller fragments that remain in the environment. Some synthetic paints contain heavy metals that can affect water quality. Decorative paints and plastic ornaments may leave residues that require post-immersion collection. A Central Pollution Control Board study conducted between 1993 and 1995 estimated that idol immersions released 32 tonnes of colours and 16.8 tonnes of varnish and garjan oil annually into the Hooghly during that period. These colours contained metals including lead, mercury and chromium, according to findings reported by Down To Earth . These are historical findings, not a measure of present-day pollution. They help explain why safer materials and careful post-immersion clean-ups matter. The CPCB's revised guidelines of May 2020 call for natural, biodegradable idols, discourage toxic synthetic paints and restrict thermocol, plastic and plaster of Paris. CPCB guidelines favour biodegradable idols and discourage thermocol, plastic and toxic paints. West Bengal's 2018 immersion rules require natural clay and bamboo, prohibit plaster of Paris and toxic colours, and place responsibilities on Puja committees and local authorities. Decorative thermocol has also been prohibited under national single-use plastic restrictions effective from July 2022. For workshops, switching materials works best when decisions are made before production begins. In August 2025, The Times of India reported that police were conducting awareness drives and inspections at Kumartuli and other idol-making centres. West Bengal's immersion rules call for natural clay and bamboo and prohibit toxic colours. Artisans interviewed for that report asked for guidance six to eight months before Durga Puja, when orders and material choices can still be changed. Koushik agrees that natural decorations need to be planned from the start. A 25-YO idol maker puts paper pulp & plant colours to the test A few workshops have already begun experimenting with alternatives. Ritwik, a 25-year-old third-generation idol maker, has been testing paper pulp for ornaments and plant-based colours for the faces of idols. After attending an awareness workshop, he brought back samples of gerua (an earth-based red pigment), turmeric-based colours and dyes derived from plants. He began trying them on small clay surfaces before using them on larger figures. "The look is different. Not worse, actually; I think it is more beautiful. But it is older-looking. Some clients like that. Some think I made a mistake. It depends on whether they know what they are seeing," he says. Artisans testing plant-based pigments say their finishes can look different from synthetic paints. The softer, slightly uneven appearance resembles the finish of traditional idols made before synthetic paints became widespread. There is no reliable figure for how many Kumartuli workshops have completely moved away from thermocol. During the reporter's visits, thermocol decorations and synthetic paints were still visible in workshops. Experiments with natural alternatives were promising, but had yet to become the norm. With thousands of idols made in Kumartuli each season, these material choices can add up. According to a September 2026 report in The Telegraph , around 166 studios produce close to 8,500 idols in a season, with turnover exceeding ₹200 crore in the previous year. A 2026 report estimated around 166 Kumartuli studios making close to 8,500 idols each season. Koushik and other artisans say a broader shift will depend on affordable traditional materials, clear specifications from buyers and guidance shared well before production begins. A reliable supply of shola, jute and natural pigments would also make it easier for workshops to plan ahead. What a painted tile shows about the choice At Gopal's workshop, a painted tile offers another way to compare the materials. One strip was coloured with synthetic paint, the other with natural pigment. Gopal left both exposed through the previous monsoon to see how they changed. The synthetic strip remained uniform; the natural one developed warmer, slightly uneven edges. Gopal did not declare either better. For him, the contrast shows how a natural finish may differ from what buyers are accustomed to. Natural pigments can create a different finish, while handmade ornaments take time. These differences need to be part of the discussion when an idol is commissioned. Traditional clay figures are moulded and dried before receiving their colours and decorations. Koushik is working to bring more of the materials his craft has long relied on back into use. Buyers can help by agreeing on materials and budgets early; timely guidance and access to affordable supplies could help more workshops do the same. Behind every idol are weeks of skilled labour. Choices about paint, decorations and post-immersion waste collection matter both to the artisans and to the river near their workshops. For Koushik, the goal is practical: honour an old craft, reduce the amount of synthetic waste entering the Hooghly and make sure artisans can still earn a fair living. items.descriptionOriginal: Flying cars are once again taking over the internet, with Tesla's plans fuelling conversations about a future where people could travel through the air instead of sitting in traffic. But in Almora, Uttarakhand, an innovator has spent 13 years working towards a similar idea, driven by a problem much closer to home. Ravi Tamta grew up in the mountains of Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham, where reaching a hospital could mean hours on winding roads. He began wondering if there was another way to travel through the hills, one that did not depend on roads or require an airport. Inspired by the challenges of reaching hospitals in the hills, Ravi Tamta spent 13 years developing a flying vehicle that can take off and land vertically. Photograph: ( Zee News) That question led him to build HAPIDA SKYNeX, an electric flying vehicle prototype that can take off and land vertically. After years of experiments, the vehicle completed its maiden test flight in August, taking off from an army helipad in Almora and remaining airborne for nearly a minute. A mountain problem sparked the idea For people living in hilly regions, distance is not always measured in kilometres. Winding roads and difficult terrain can turn a relatively short journey into a long trip, particularly when someone needs medical attention. Tamta began exploring whether a flying vehicle could help people cover such distances faster. His idea was to develop a vehicle that could rise vertically, travel over difficult terrain, and land without needing a runway. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The aim is to make air travel more accessible in hilly regions, particularly during medical emergencies and in areas that are difficult to reach by road. Developed under his venture, Hapida Sky Private Limited, the HAPIDA SKYNeX combines modified, scaled-up multirotor drone technology with an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) system. In simple terms, it uses the same basic principle that lets a multirotor drone take off and hover, but applies it to a prototype designed to carry a person. Unlike conventional aircraft that need a runway to gain enough speed for take-off, an eVTOL vehicle is designed to lift off and land vertically. This could make the technology particularly relevant to mountainous areas, where finding suitable space for runways can be difficult. How the flying vehicle works HAPIDA SKYNeX uses multiple electric motors and propellers mounted on external arms to generate lift. Working together, these components are designed to raise the vehicle off the ground, sustain a hover, and help control its movement through the air. This multirotor arrangement is similar in principle to the technology used in drones, although scaling it up to carry a person presents additional engineering and safety challenges. The prototype also features a lightweight frame, a cockpit designed for a single pilot and a transparent canopy. Its electric propulsion system is battery-powered, eliminating direct exhaust emissions during operation. From a mobile-charging shoe to a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, Ravi Tamta's earlier inventions also focused on solving practical, everyday problems. Photograph: ( Business Today ) However, its practical flight range, battery endurance, and overall efficiency will depend on factors such as the battery capacity, the vehicle's weight, and the power required to sustain flight. The intended use is short-distance travel across difficult terrain. According to the reported project details, a journey of around 40 kilometres that takes approximately 90 minutes by mountain road could potentially be completed in 10 to 15 minutes by air. This is an intended travel-time goal, rather than a demonstrated operational capability at this stage. Thirteen years of learning through experiments Tamta did not have an engineering degree or access to a fancy laboratory. Instead, he turned to the internet to learn, relying on his parents' support and repeated experiments to develop his idea. Over 13 years, the concept gradually took shape under his venture, Hapida Skynex. The maiden flight was an important step in testing whether his idea could work beyond the drawing board. The single-seater prototype features a lightweight frame, a cockpit for one pilot and a transparent canopy, with multiple electric motors and propellers designed to generate lift. Photograph: ( Influencer Book of World Records ) The prototype is still at an early stage and requires further testing. While the test flight offers a glimpse of what the vehicle might eventually do, it is too soon to know how it will perform in regular use. Before a vehicle of this kind can be used for routine passenger travel, it would need to demonstrate reliable flight control, sufficient battery performance, structural stability and safe responses to component failures. Operating in mountainous terrain would bring additional considerations, including changing weather, wind conditions, landing-site availability and emergency procedures. From everyday inventions to flying vehicles The flying vehicle is not Tamta's first attempt at solving practical problems through invention. His earlier creations include shoes that charge mobile phones on the go, a smart walking stick for visually impaired people, a bamboo-splitting machine and firefighting equipment. Ravi Tamta hopes HAPIDA SKYNeX will one day make travel across Uttarakhand's mountains faster and more accessible. Photograph: ( Instagram/@ravi_tamta3 ) Each project began with a practical challenge, leading him to explore how a device could make a task easier. HAPIDA SKYNeX has a longer journey ahead before it can carry passengers or help people reach hospitals faster. For now, its first flight marks a step forward for an idea shaped by life in the mountains. As conversations about flying cars continue online, Tamta's work offers a different way to look at the technology: not just as a futuristic mode of transport, but as a possible answer to the everyday challenges of getting from one place to another. Sources: 'Uttarakhand Man Conducts Test Flight Of Drone-Based Flying Vehicle: Watch' by NDTV, Published on 8 August 2026. 'This Uttarakhand youth built an electric flying vehicle. Here's why everyone is talking about Ravi Tamta' by The Times of India, Published on 7 August 2026.
