items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The innovative approach of Ocean Cleanup Reading Time: 4 minutes From a Dutch teenager’s question in 2013 to 50 million kilograms of debris removed, Ocean Cleanup proves ingenuity can still tackle one of the ocean’s most overwhelming problems. Our oceans cover 71% of the planet’s surface, plunging down nearly 11,000 meters at their deepest point in the Mariana Trench, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Below the waves lies home to billions of species spread across coral reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass beds, and hydrothermal vents. The deep-sea bed alone hosts an estimated 500,000 to 10 million species, with scientists believing 91% of ocean species remain unclassified to this day. Despite this astounding biodiversity, humans continue to put large portions of it at risk with persistent detrimental activities. In 2023, the 5 Gyres Institute, set up by Marcus Eriksen and Anna Cummings to carry out in-depth research on plastic pollution, published data revealing that 82-358 trillion plastic particles currently float on the ocean’s surface, equal to between 2.4 and 4.9 million tonnes. However, this figure is only the portion of plastic that floats; the United Nations Regional Information Centre for Western Europe (UNRIC) estimates that in total from rivers, lakes and oceans, between nine and 23 million tonnes of plastic waste reach aquatic ecosystems annually. These are the statistics that led Boyan Slat, at the age of only 18, to ask himself why no real progress was being made to tackle the plastics that had found their way into our world’s seas. In 2013, Slat set up Ocean Cleanup, which has now grown into a globally recognized non-profit organisation that utilises sustainable innovation to systematically clear non-biodegradable waste from oceans. The idea was brought to life when the Dutch innovator designed a system that harnesses the natural movement of waves and currents to push plastic into the curve of a U-shaped inflatable barrier which floats on the ocean’s surface, with both ends steered by a boat. Once the retention zone is full, it is detached from the main inflatable system, emptied into a third boat and replaced, continuing the process. The plastics on board the collection boat are taken back to shore and recycled. At 18, Boyan Slat designed a U-shaped floating barrier that uses natural wave and current movement to concentrate ocean plastic into a collection zone, creating the foundation of what Ocean Cleanup has become today. Photo courtesy of Ocean Cleanup . A perfected process now allows the organization to use an Automated Debris Imaging System (ADIS), which not only keeps track of plastic collected, but also monitors and maps the distribution of plastic debris using embedded AI. This helps to plot where to place their cleanup systems as efficiently as possible. The crew onboard also includes independent observers to monitor interactions with marine life, such as protected turtle species or whales. The key to the design is that ocean animals can easily swim under or around the system without harm. The retention zone has numerous inbuilt safety measures, including acoustic deterrents, escape aids for any animals caught up in the rubbish, and breathing hatches for mammals to ensure they can access a clear patch of ocean surface. In 2025, Ocean Cleanup launched System 03, which is almost three times larger than previous systems and measures up to 2.2km long, hoping to make even more impact on the effects of the climate crisis. The organisation has found that ocean plastics accumulate mainly in five different zones called ocean garbage patches, the biggest of them all being the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. This is bounded by the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, a network of ocean currents, which rotates clockwise around an area of 20 million square kilometres. As the currents churn the plastics piled up in the Patch, they break down further, becoming microplastics which are known to build up in food chains that are reaching humans. Turtles are eating plastic bags mistaking them for jellyfish, albatrosses are feeding resin pellets to young instead of fish eggs, and a phenomenon known as ‘ghost fishing’ is becoming ever more common as marine mammals get tangled in discarded plastic fishing nets. This is why this Patch has become a main target zone for the organisation. However, by weight 70-80% of ocean plastic actually arrives there by rivers, with studies suggesting that just a few major rivers are the worst offenders. This is why Ocean Cleanup tackles the root of the problem as well, working with government leaders, individuals and private companies to set up interceptors at points along some of the most polluted rivers, like the Sandy Gully in Kingston, Jamaica. These interceptors include barriers, barricades, guards and the Interceptor Original: an autonomous, 100% solar powered craft that utilises a conveyor belt to continuously extract debris and distribute it evenly between containers that can store up to 50m 3 of trash combined before needing to be emptied. All of which work together to drastically reduce the trash flow from rivers into the wider sea. In March 2026, Ocean Cleanup reached 50 million kg of debris removed. This organization is living proof that with perseverance and ingenious solutions we can come together to tackle some of our world’s largest problems. But how can you play your part to help reduce plastics in our oceans? So how can you help reduce plastic in our oceans? Every little bit counts. Refuse single-use plastics like straws, and bring reusable bags when you shop. Recycle properly, following your local program’s rules closely. Avoid microbeads in products like face scrubs, usually listed as “polyethylene” or “polypropylene” on ingredient labels. Share what you’ve learned with others. Support organizations fighting plastic pollution. Join a river or beach cleanup, and never flush non-biodegradable items down the toilet. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis Reading Time: 3 minutes Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts in Mexico’s Chihuahuan Desert are reviving ancient pools and returning bison to the land, offering a model for desert restoration worldwide. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation begins in a valley most people have never heard of. Tucked into the Chihuahuan Desert in Coahuila, the basin holds hundreds of crystal-clear pools called pozas that Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has spent years working to protect. These pools support life found nowhere else on the planet. The valley became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2006. It spans more than 413,000 hectares, an area larger than Los Angeles. Within that space live over 800 plant species and roughly 360 animal species, many found only here. The pools themselves hold something even stranger. Scientists have traced microbial life in the pozas back nearly 500 million years. Researchers believe these microbes descended from an ancient sea trapped underground when mountains rose around the basin. Some pozas also contain stromatolites, layered rock structures built by microbial colonies. Scientists consider them living relatives of some of Earth’s earliest life forms, similar to formations found in Australia’s Shark Bay. Few places on the planet still host stromatolites forming under natural conditions today. Mexican scientists Valeria Souza and Luis Eguiarte made that discovery, turning a quiet desert valley into a living laboratory. Their work found more bacterial diversity in a single pool than scientists had documented across China’s entire Pearl River. The find helped convince Mexico to take the area’s protection more seriously. Protection came just in time. Decades of irrigation for alfalfa farming, much of it feeding dairy operations, drained the aquifer feeding the pozas. Nearly 90 percent of the valley’s surface water has disappeared since the 1960s. Churince, once the basin’s largest lagoon, dried up completely in 2016. That loss sparked a wave of local action. In 2018, conservationists won a court order forcing officials to close a canal draining two major pools. The ruling marked a turning point for regional water policy. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas has since built on that momentum, becoming the driving force behind on-the-ground Cuatro Ciénegas conservation. The nonprofit works to protect the valley’s water, restore native habitat, and support ranching methods that use less water. Its programs also train local students in environmental science, turning former skeptics into active partners in the valley’s recovery. That shift in local support matters. Many families once saw conservation as a threat to their livelihoods. Years of education and dialogue changed that view for many residents, who now see healthy pozas as tied to their own future. The clearest sign of progress arrived in December 2025. Forty-four American bison arrived at a reserve called El Santuario in Coahuila, marking a major step in Cuatro Ciénegas conservation efforts. The animals came from a managed herd at Rancho El Uno in Chihuahua’s Janos Biosphere Reserve, overseen by the conservation group Cuenca Los Ojos. American bison graze on restored grassland in Coahuila, part of a new Cuatro Ciénegas conservation effort to bring the keystone species back to northern Mexico. Photo courtesy of Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas . Bison do more than roam grasslands. Their grazing improves soil structure and helps native plants recover. Unlike cattle, bison tolerate drought well, making them a natural fit for a region growing hotter and drier. The project brought together Mexico’s environment ministry, SEMARNAT, along with its national parks commission, CONANP, and several conservation groups. Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas partnered with the N’dee/N’nee/Ndé Indigenous nation to open reserve land for the herd. The Mexican Fund for the Conservation of Nature also supported the effort, reflecting the broad coalition needed to pull off a reintroduction of this scale. Officials involved called the partnership a model for Cuatro Ciénegas conservation going forward. Government agencies, scientists, ranchers, and Indigenous communities rarely align this closely. Their shared success offers a template other desert regions could follow. Cuatro Ciénegas conservation still faces real challenges. Water rights in Mexico remain tangled in overlapping laws, and some irrigation canals draining the basin remain open. Full recovery of dried lagoons like Churince could take years, if it happens at all. Even so, the signs of resilience are hard to ignore. Researchers have found that dormant microbes can survive in dry mud for years, springing back to life once water returns. A desert valley that nearly vanished is showing what patient, collaborative Cuatro Ciénegas conservation can achieve. Scientists study its microbes, ranchers adjust old habits, students learn to protect their backyard, and American bison once again roam land shaped by their ancestors. What happens next in Cuatro Ciénegas may show the rest of the world how to save a dying ecosystem before it is too late. The post Cuatro Ciénegas Conservation Restores Mexico’s Ancient Desert Oasis appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Happy Eco News Το Urban Food Forest μεταμορφώνει τους ουρανοξύστες της Σιγκαπούρης σε βρώσιμα τοπία Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 3 λεπτά Ένα αστικό δάσος τροφίμων ευδοκιμεί 51 ορόφους πάνω από τους δρόμους της Σιγκαπούρης, αποδεικνύοντας ότι οι υπερπυκνές πόλεις μπορούν να αναπτυχθούν πολύ περισσότερο από το διακοσμητικό πράσινο. Ο εκπαιδευτής Permaculture Andrew Millison ταξίδεψε στη Σιγκαπούρη για να απαντήσει σε μια απατηλά απλή ερώτηση…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes Reading Time: 3 minutes An urban food forest thrives 51 floors above Singapore’s streets, proving hyperdense cities can grow far more than ornamental greenery. Permaculture educator Andrew Millison traveled to Singapore to answer a deceptively simple question: how much food, greenery, and habitat can a hyperdense urban environment actually produce? What he found reshaped his understanding of what cities can grow. At the top of one Singapore skyscraper sits what is described as the world’s highest rooftop farm, an urban food forest producing roughly a ton of organic food annually on the 51st floor. Bananas, mulberries, star fruit, and water apples grow alongside pumpkin vines. Bees pollinate crops despite the extreme elevation, including kadong , a native fruit with a tart, green-apple flavor whose edible leaves are traditionally used in local salads. A nearby miracle berry temporarily transforms sour flavors into sweet ones, delighting visitors encountering the effect for the first time. Unlike conventional rooftop farms arranged in single horizontal rows of vegetables, this urban food forest layers vertically within a tight footprint. Tree layers rise above shrub layers, herbs fill the understory, and vines climb through the structure, creating a legitimate multi-tiered food production system rather than a novelty garden. The restaurant sourcing from this rooftop describes the space as inseparable from its culinary philosophy, using every part of each harvest to minimize waste while drawing creative inspiration directly from what grows above the kitchen. Beyond this single example, Millison explored how urban food forest principles could scale across Singapore’s built environment. The island nation has almost no farmland and imports nearly all of its food, yet government policy already mandates extensive greenery integration. A landscape replacement policy requires developers to replace any land they build on with equivalent greenery elsewhere on the structure, driving widespread adoption of vertical gardens and rooftop plantings across the city. One striking example of this policy in action covers roughly 200% of its building footprint in combined horizontal and vertical greenery, effectively treating the high-rise as a small mountain, with the ground extending upward through multiple stories. The landscape architect behind the design explained that root space is the central engineering challenge, requiring sufficient soil depth or widened planters, root barriers to prevent structural damage, built-in drainage systems, maintenance walkways, and anchor cables to stabilize mature tree canopies as they grow denser over time. Currently, Singapore maintains roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space, but most of this greenery consists of exotic ornamental plants rather than food-producing species. The country spends approximately one billion dollars annually managing this urban vegetation. Replacing ornamental plantings with productive alternatives, while maintaining the same underlying infrastructure, could transform this investment into a genuine urban food forest network spanning the entire city, rather than a purely decorative one. Singapore’s landscape replacement policy has created roughly 2,000 hectares of green rooftop space citywide, with Edible Garden City working to transform this largely ornamental urban food forest infrastructure into a genuine perennial food production network using resilient native and traditional crops. Photo by Cyrill on Pexels. Edible Garden City, a Singapore-based urban farming social enterprise, is actively developing the plant genetics needed to make this transition possible. At Gardens by the Bay, the organization experiments with diversified, multi-tiered plantings that move away from monoculture rows toward genuine food forest design. This approach reduces pest pressure by diluting concentrated crops across diverse species, minimizes pesticide use, and incorporates flowering plants that attract pollinators while producing edible blooms. Perennial plants form the backbone of this urban food forest model, since street-side and terrace plantings cannot practically be tilled and replanted annually like conventional vegetable plots. Species proven successful at the test site are introduced to industry partners and community gardens, spreading resilient, low-maintenance crops including lemongrass, pandan, cassava, sweet potato, and Brazilian spinach, alongside traditional vegetables once grown by earlier generations before industrial food systems replaced them. Singapore currently allocates only about 1% of its land to farming, yet its extensive rooftop and vertical greening infrastructure suggests far greater capacity remains untapped. The research, plant trials, and structural engineering needed to convert ornamental cityscapes into a genuine urban food forest have already been completed and proven at scale within the city itself, requiring policy rather than new invention for wider implementation. What makes Singapore’s example significant extends beyond any single rooftop or building. The city demonstrates that food production and dense urban living are not inherently incompatible, provided cities are willing to reimagine landscaping budgets, structural design, and plant selection around productivity rather than appearance alone. An urban food forest at this scale offers a template other hyperdense cities worldwide could adapt, transforming skylines already covered in decorative greenery into genuine sources of food, habitat, and community resilience. The post Urban Food Forest Transforms Singapore’s Skyscrapers into Edible Landscapes appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Το Κάλεσμα είναι Πραγματικό
items.titleOriginal: The Call is Real
items.description: Ο Emanuel Kuntzelman έχει ιδιαίτερη σχέση με τα δέντρα. Καθισμένος σε μια μηλιά σε ηλικία έξι ετών, αποφάσισε να αφιερώσει τη ζωή του στην υπηρεσία του σύμπαντος. Κάτω από μια βελανιδιά στο κολέγιο, διατύπωσε μια ιδέα για να ενώσει τους ανθρώπους σε έναν κοινό σκοπό. Διαβάζοντας κάτω από μια ιτιά που κλαίει, του ήρθε το όνομα Holomovement για αυτόν τον κοινό σκοπό, ένα κίνημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Emanuel Kuntzelman has a special relationship with trees. Sitting in an apple tree at the early age of six, he decided to dedicate his life to serving the universe. Under an oak in college, he formulated an idea to unite people in a common purpose. Reading under a weeping willow, the name Holomovement came to him for that common purpose, a movement he later helped realize. People also appeared along the way as if on cue to point him in a direction when he didn’t know which way he was going. “Sometimes the universe makes things so easy for us — if you're on that quest for truth, and you're willing to say it here and there.” Emanuel believes each person has a calling, a purpose, and trees and people are there to help us as long as we keep learning and seeking. In doing so, all can join in the Holomovement “to unite humanity through our collective purpose.”

Το Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) ανέφερε σχετικά με μια σειρά συναντήσεων ενδιαφερομένων που διοργανώθηκαν από τον εταίρο του για τη διατήρηση, την Εταιρεία Προστασίας Οφιοφάουνας και…
items.descriptionOriginal: In November 2018, conservationists working in North Bengal's Dooars region raised an alarm about a barrier that was increasingly obstructing elephants: razor-sharp fencing around tea estates. The Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) reported on a series of stakeholder meetings organised by its conservation partner, the Society for Protecting Ophiofauna and Animal Rights (SPOAR), between 11 and 16 November that year. It described how randomly installed razor-blade fencing was forcing elephant herds to divert from their usual routes. The organisation reported that the sharp wires caused serious injuries to elephants and other wildlife, and that some animals died while attempting to cross the fences. The report did not identify individual animals or provide a tally of razor-wire injuries . But it highlighted a problem that extended beyond the fences themselves: when elephants could no longer follow familiar routes, their movement could bring them into closer contact with people. In August 2026, WTI and SPOAR brought tea estate representatives, government agencies and conservation organisations together in Chalsa, Jalpaiguri, to discuss elephant-friendly management. Photograph: (csmonitor) Seven years later, a reassessment by WTI and SPOAR would offer a measurable indication of how much the landscape had changed. Between 2019 and 2026, the length of razor-wire fencing mapped across the assessed tea-estate landscape fell from approximately 134.7 km to 34.8 km, a reduction of 74.2%. The change followed years of engagement with tea estate management, local communities and government agencies. It also raised a question: how much safer can an elephant's journey become when a landscape begins to accommodate its movement? A corridor is not always a forest Across North Bengal's Terai and Duars, elephant movement does not stop at the edge of a forest. Routes run through forest patches, tea plantations, worker settlements, roads and railway lines. These connections allow elephants to move between habitats in search of food, water and space. But when land is divided by fences, trenches and other obstacles, a familiar passage can become difficult or dangerous to navigate. For tea estates, fencing may be intended to protect workers, crops and property. Yet barriers placed across elephant movement routes can also redirect herds towards labour lines, roads and settlements, creating risks for people and wildlife alike. To understand the extent of the problem, WTI and SPOAR conducted a year-long field survey in 2019 across eight identified elephant corridors in North Bengal. The survey documented how elephants used tea estates and identified barriers that could impede their movement. From a survey to a shared commitment The findings became the starting point for discussions with those managing the landscape. On World Elephant Day in August 2019, nearly 50 representatives from tea estates, the Forest Department , tea associations, the administration and conservation organisations gathered for a consultative workshop on securing elephant passage through tea gardens. The discussions focused on practical measures such as identifying problematic barriers, keeping movement routes open and reducing losses for both people and elephants. Camera trap footage of a wild #elephant herd crossing the Apalchand-Kalimpong corridor via the Meenglass Tea Estate in North Bengal. These cameras were installed by WTI's Green Corridor Champion (GCC) partner in the landscape, @SPOAR_India https://t.co/ZF4RgSGE3a — Wildlife Trust of India (@wti_org_india) November 22, 2024 Some tea estate representatives shared examples of areas being left open for elephants. Others discussed commitments to remove existing razor wire or to avoid installing it in the future. WTI, SPOAR, the Forest Department and tea estate management continued engaging with the landscape, while awareness initiatives helped workers and residents understand elephant movement and the risks posed by obstructed routes. What changed between 2019 and 2026? A reassessment by WTI and SPOAR in 2026 offered a way to measure changes in the fencing landscape. In 2019, the survey had mapped 291.7 km of fencing across the assessed area. By 2026, the total had fallen to 104.5 km. The decline in razor-wire fencing was particularly notable in 2026: from 134.7 km to 34.8 km. However, the figures do not mean that all the missing fencing was deliberately removed. WTI's account attributes the reduction to a combination of removal, deterioration and fencing not being reinstalled. Nor do the figures establish how many elephant injuries or h uman-elephant encounters have been prevented. They measure a change in the physical barriers across the landscape, not a verified reduction in casualties. Still, the reassessment suggests that estate practices have changed over time, following sustained engagement and discussions about safer elephant movement. The next danger is overhead The same reassessment identified another concern: low-hanging electrical infrastructure. The survey documented 54 power lines below a height of 13 feet, with 47.4% hanging below 10 feet. These were flagged as serious hazards to elephants. An elephant may be able to move past a fence only to encounter a low electrical line or another obstacle along its route. The findings are intended to guide joint verification and corrective action involving tea estate management, the Forest Department, the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL) and conservation partners. A charter for coexistence In August 2026, WTI and SPOAR brought tea estate representatives, government agencies and conservation organisations together in Chalsa, Jalpaiguri, to discuss elephant-friendly management. The consultation introduced the Elephant-Friendly Tea Estate Charter. The proposed framework focuses on keeping known elephant routes open, reviewing hazardous fencing , improving electrical safety, preparing workers and residents for encounters, managing crowds and strengthening monitoring. The fall from 134.7 km to 34.8 km of razor-wire fencing is a measurable change. It is not, on its own, proof that elephants are safer. Establishing that will require continued monitoring of injuries, deaths, movement patterns and encounters with people. Sources: 'SPOAR lobbies to Mitigate Human-Elephant Conflict in Elephant Corridors of Dooars in Northern West Bengal' : By WTI 'From Commitments to Change: How North Bengal's Tea Estates are Making Space for Elephants' : By Upasana Ganguly, Published on 8 October 2026

items.description: «Νωρίτερα, ήταν πολύ δύσκολο για μένα», λέει ο κάτοικος της Μπανγκαλούρου, Rashmi Sampath, θυμούμενος κάθε οικογενειακή έξοδο με τη 16χρονη κόρη της, Deeksha, η οποία έχει μυϊκή ατροφία της σπονδυλικής στήλης. "Ζυγίζει 55 κιλά και το να τη σηκώσεις στο αυτοκίνητο ήταν εξουθενωτικό. Τώρα όμως, αφού το κάθισμα περιστρέφεται 90 μοίρες, είναι πολύ άνετο." Η διαφορά ήταν mo…
items.descriptionOriginal: "Earlier, it was very difficult for me," says Bengaluru resident Rashmi Sampath, recalling every family outing with her 16-year-old daughter, Deeksha, who has spinal muscular atrophy. "She weighs 55 kilograms, and lifting her into the car was exhausting. But now, since the seat rotates 90 degrees, it is very comfortable." The difference has been more than convenience. A journey that once demanded careful planning, physical effort, and frequent compromises has become something the family can look forward to. Last year, they drove nearly 1,000 kilometres from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari without the travel itself becoming an obstacle. "She was very comfortable throughout," Rashmi says. "We took just two breaks. She could even sleep on the seat. Earlier, we couldn't have imagined travelling such a long distance like this." For millions of Indians living with disabilities or age-related mobility challenges, the hardest part of a journey often begins before the vehicle even starts moving. Getting into a car can require multiple people, unsafe lifting techniques, or simply deciding that the trip isn't worth the effort. It is this overlooked challenge that Bengaluru-based TRUE Assistive Technology set out to address. Founded by engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre, the company designs assistive mobility solutions, including swivel seats, portable ramps, transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle modifications, that make everyday travel safer and more accessible. TurnPlus rotates towards the car door, making it easier for passengers to get in and out with less physical strain. Since beginning its journey, the company says it has enabled mobility for over 1,000 users across India, supporting people with conditions ranging from paralysis and Parkinson's disease to post-polio complications and age-related mobility issues. A project that uncovered a larger problem Neither Naina nor Anand had initially planned to build an assistive technology company. Both spent over two decades working as engineers — Naina in software and compliance engineering, Anand in the automotive sector. Their journey into accessible mobility began unexpectedly in 2013, when Toyota approached them with a project to design a swivel seat for the Corolla Altis. The prototype was showcased at an auto show, but it failed to gain traction because of its high cost. "We went on to see how we could bring the solution to the Indian market," recalls Naina. Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre spent years developing mobility solutions that work with existing cars, without permanent modifications. The idea had also been shaped by another experience. Having lived in the United States before returning to India, the couple had seen people with disabilities participating independently in everyday life. "We had seen a lot of people in the US who were disabled but still living day-to-day life with full potential. We thought we should do something similar in India," she says. The path, however, was anything but straightforward. Without external funding, they bootstrapped the venture using income from consulting assignments. "Sometimes we had money but no people, and sometimes we had people but no funds," Anand recalls. "That's why it took about four years to bring the whole thing together." Interest slowly began building after an article about their work led families to reach out directly. Once they had served their first hundred customers, the founders realised there was a genuine demand for accessible mobility solutions in India. They expanded the design to fit nearly 80 percent of Indian car models before formally establishing TRUE Assistive Technology in 2022. Designing for Indian conditions As Anand began designing the products, one principle remained non-negotiable. "I didn't want to do anything like jugaad ," he says. Instead of permanently altering vehicles, the founders focused on creating solutions that could fit existing cars without affecting warranties, insurance, or resale value. Their flagship innovation, TurnPlus , is a patented swivel-seat mechanism that transforms an existing car seat into one that rotates outward. Rather than climbing or being lifted awkwardly into the vehicle, the passenger can first sit on the seat while it faces the door. The seat then swivels back into the cabin, making transfers smoother for senior citizens and people with conditions such as paralysis, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, post-polio complications and spinal injuries. Unlike many vehicle modifications that require structural changes, TurnPlus uses the car's existing seat. The mechanism is installed beneath it, allowing the seat to rotate without permanently altering the vehicle. TRUE Assistive Technology's portable ramps and transfer systems help wheelchair users navigate everyday barriers at home and on the move. "We didn't want people to leave their vehicles in garages for days," Naina explains. "You don't have to leave the vehicle with us. We bring the product to your doorstep." Because the original seat remains intact, the system can also be removed later if the owner decides to sell the vehicle, helping preserve its resale value. As they worked with more users, the founders realised that mobility challenges rarely end once someone gets into a car. Some wheelchair users needed a safer way to enter vehicles without being manually lifted. Others struggled with small staircases outside homes, clinics or public buildings. That led to the development of RamPlus , a lightweight portable ramp that can be carried in a vehicle and unfolded whenever a step or raised entrance blocks wheelchair access. The company later introduced TransPlus and HoistPlus , assistive systems and transferring devices that help caregivers lift and transfer people safely between wheelchairs, beds and vehicles, reducing physical strain for both users and families. For individuals who require more extensive support, TRUE also undertakes end-to-end vehicle modifications, including wheelchair ramps, hydraulic lifts and roof-height adjustments that convert standard vehicles into wheelchair-accessible ones. Before reaching users, every solution undergoes automotive safety testing, including front and rear crash tests, seat belt anchorage testing and durability assessments across temperatures ranging from minus 20 C to plus 60 C. The above tests are only for their products and not for vehicle modifications. "If I had to sell it across India , it had to be as reliable as the vehicle itself," Anand says. 'To be dependent on anybody is very painful' For Amritsar resident Jatin Gandotra, the technology came into his life after someone close to him suffered a stroke. His relative, now in her 60s, has severely restricted mobility and has spent nearly two years confined to bed. Jatin first discovered TRUE Assistive Technology while reading about a collaboration with Maruti Suzuki. "I found the technology very fascinating because my close relative is a stroke patient," he says. "I wanted to see how we could help her." After a relative suffered a stroke, Jatin Gandotra turned to accessible mobility to make family outings easier for her. Today, the family uses TurnPlus to help her get into the car more comfortably. Speaking about the emotional impact, Jatin says it goes far beyond the physical act of travelling. "To be dependent upon anybody is very, very painful," he says. "When you look through the patient's eyes, you can see that satisfaction that they are being cared for." For him, accessible mobility is ultimately about giving families more choices. "See what freedom you can bring to their life," he says. More than easier journeys The founders say stories like these continue to reinforce why they chose this path. Among their earliest customers was a woman who completed her PhD sooner because she could travel to college more frequently after installing the mobility solution. Another user, Vijay Kannan, fulfilled a long-held dream of driving his parents to Ayodhya after equipping his vehicle with an accessible ramp. "It's not just for the person using it," says Naina. "It helps the entire family. When they see how conveniently they can travel together, it changes things for everyone." Rashmi has witnessed that change firsthand. "The more we socialise these children, the happier they become," she says. "We shouldn't confine them to a single room." Her daughter now plans trips with the confidence many teenagers take for granted. "She says, 'We'll go anywhere. We'll explore this place.' She feels nothing is limited for her anymore." For families like Rashmi's, accessible mobility means fewer limitations, more shared experiences and the freedom to explore the world beyond their homes. According to the Census 2011, India is home to over 2.68 crore persons with disabilities, alongside a rapidly growing elderly population. Yet for many, something as ordinary as getting into a vehicle remains one of the biggest barriers to participating in everyday life. For families like Rashmi's and Jatin's, accessible mobility is not simply about modifying a car. It means visiting relatives without anxiety, travelling to school or work more comfortably, taking a long-awaited road trip, or stepping outside after months of staying indoors. Sometimes, restoring independence begins with making the first step into a vehicle a little easier. All images courtesy True Assistive Technology team

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall, something happens in the body before it happens in the mind. The smell of wood smoke drifting through a cracked window, the particular weight of October light slanting across the floor, and suddenly you’re somewhere else entirely, back in a kitchen you haven’t thought about in years, or feeling fourteen again for no apparent reason. Then you reach for the show you always watch this time of year, or the book with the cracked spine, and the evening softens. If that pull toward the familiar feels like something you should probably resist, it isn’t. Mental health professionals describe what happens each autumn as a predictable response to something real: the season changing registers in your nervous system as a small form of loss. The nostalgia that follows isn’t a distraction from fall; rather, it’s a part of how you move through it. Seasonal transitions are a form of small loss “Transitions mean something is changing, and change inherently means something is being lost,” says Janna Sayfie , L.M.S.W., co-founder and psychotherapist at Urban Mind Psychotherapy. “These ‘endings,’ however small, register to us as a form of loss. Looking back at something familiar anchors us to a sense of continuity and stability that we try to find when it feels like the ground is shifting beneath us.” That sense of loss takes different shapes for different people. For a lot of adults, the end of summer is the end of a looser way of moving through the week, a rhythm that’s harder to hold onto once September arrives. For parents, back-to-school season carries a weight that’s difficult to articulate, the passage of time made suddenly visible. And even without children in the picture, fall tends to settle in with a certain pressure attached: fresh starts implied, intentions expected, a vague sense that you should be doing more with the season than you are. Matt Sosnowsky , L.C.S.W., founder and psychotherapist at Philadelphia Talk Therapy, compares it to New Year’s, with all the same weight and none of the festivities. Your body recognizes fall before your brain does Part of why autumn nostalgia can feel so sudden and strange is that it often bypasses the thinking mind entirely. Sarah Haugh , L.M.H.C., founder of North Shore Professional Therapy, describes these as somatic memories: body-based recall that surfaces through sensory cues before any conscious recognition has kicked in. “Even before we know what these triggers remind us of, we’re swept away into visceral or nervous system memory,” Haugh says. She explains that this kind of implicit memory, a felt sense rather than a story you can retrieve, is the same part of the memory system that holds experiences from before we had language. Fall is unusually thick with these triggers. Wood smoke through a cracked window. The low angle of October light that somehow reads as different from September even when the temperature hasn’t shifted. Damp leaves, a candle you only bring out once a year, the sound of a school bus on a Tuesday morning. Any of these can pull a decade-old feeling into your chest before you’ve had a chance to ask where it came from. Why reruns feel better than something new Once the nervous system has registered the season as a kind of ending, it tends to steer toward the known. Sayfie puts it plainly: “Our brains tend to favor the predictable over the unpredictable.” We associate the unknown with risk, and when things are shifting, even in the small seasonal way they do every year, the familiar offers something new experiences can’t: you already know how it ends. Revisiting a favorite show or book is one way of meeting that need without quite naming it. The characters feel like company you trust. There’s no uncertainty about whether it will be good. Sosnowsky describes this as a form of safety-seeking, not a failure to engage with what’s ahead, but a way of steadying yourself so that you can. Nostalgia as a tool, not just a feeling Sosnowsky calls nostalgia “an engine for positive emotions,” pointing to research showing that wellbeing draws from three sources: anticipating the future, savoring the present, and looking back at the past. “Taking time to sink into a memory with gratitude and appreciation can help us elevate seminal experiences of joy, connection, and deep meaning,” he says. Nostalgia works that third channel. Don’t think of it as wallowing but as a return to something that still has something to give. Sometimes it carries grief alongside the warmth, which is its own kind of usefulness. A young person packing for college while their mind keeps wandering back to high school. A parent watching a kid start middle school while some part of them is still at kindergarten drop-off. Someone moving through a first round of holidays without a person they love. Looking backward in these moments isn’t getting stuck; it’s how the past gets processed. “Looking back, though sometimes difficult, helps us to integrate our past and make meaning from life,” Sosnowsky says. “In this way, we benefit from the people, places, and experiences that helped shape our lives by recognizing what remains a part of us as we move forward.” So when October settles in, and you find yourself scrolling down to the same playlist, reaching for the same worn-out novel, or clicking on the same show you’ve already seen more times than you can count, that pull isn’t something to override. It may be your nervous system holding onto who you are while the season changes around you. Remind yourself that you can gift yourself that return. At some point, when you’re ready, you can always put something new on. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.title: Η ψηλότερη ανεμογεννήτρια στον κόσμο φτάνει τα 1.197 πόδια στη Γερμανία
items.titleOriginal: World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Η ψηλότερη ανεμογεννήτρια στον κόσμο μόλις έφτασε σε πλήρες ύψος στη Γερμανία. Ο πιλοτικός στρόβιλος της GICON στο Schipkau, στην ανατολική Γερμανία, έχει τώρα ύψος 365 μέτρα (1.197 πόδια) από τη βάση μέχρι την άκρη του πτερυγίου, καθιστώντας τον τη δεύτερη ψηλότερη κατασκευή της Γερμανίας μετά τον πύργο της τηλεόρασης του Βερολίνου. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. The plan is to stack them above. A “second tier” of tall turbines with their rotors spinning above those of conventional turbines already in the ground, adding generation without touching any new land. Germany’s existing wind farms could potentially fit up to 4,000 of them, per the companies’ own estimate. That’s a significant amount of added capacity without a single new wind farm permit. The Schipkau turbine is still a pilot, and the yield projections haven’t been proven in operation yet. GICON and SPRIND are in talks with wind energy companies about commercialization, with series production as the goal. Everything depends on what the numbers look like once it’s running. items.descriptionOriginal: A married California couple has made it their mission to photograph all 40 wild cat species on Earth — and they only have one more to go. The stunning images serve to raise awareness about the animals, many of which are vulnerable or endangered. So far, Sebastian Kennerknecht and Rachel Tobias have traveled to 33 countries across five continents and photographed 39 species in the Felidae family, often using camera traps in forests, deserts, and grasslands where the elusive cats roam. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht The San Francisco-based duo has captured images of a cheetah in Tanzania, a tiger in India, and an ocelot in Panama. The only species they have yet to cross off the list is the northern oncilla, found in Central America. It’s a rarely seen animal, and one of smallest wild cats in the Americas. View this post on Instagram Kennerknecht, 41, has been photographing cats since college: He studied ecology at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to understand animals and became particularly interested in bobcats. Tobias, 37, grew up loving wildlife and was always drawn to the ocean and photography. The two met online, and they instantly connected over their love of nature. Fittingly, their first date was searching for bobcats. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht In 2024, Kennerknecht realized he had photos of 30 of the world’s wild cats, so he and Tobias decided to go for the full 40. In addition to photography, the couple run cat expeditions together, taking out small groups to observe the felines in their natural habitat and learn how to photograph them. They’ve raised hundreds of thousands of dollars through their work. One photo of a Borneo Bay cat brought in $120,000 for conservation efforts, and they collected around $70,000 per year for five years to protect lion species in Zambia’s Kafue National Park. They are partnered with Panthera, the world’s leading wild cat conservation organization. Kennerknecht told Talk to the Press that the couple’s work is “99% frustration and 1% joy,” noting that they’ve seen elephants crush their expensive camera traps, insects get into them, and humidity fog up lenses, rendering images unusable. “We set up a studio in the forest,” Tobias explained, adding: “In Malaysia, we set up six traps; we had to sleep in the jungle full of bugs and carry 60 pounds of gear.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Despite the project’s challenges, the couple is dedicated to ethical photography. They don’t use any bait or lures to attract the cats towards the cameras, so they can observe their natural behavior. “It’s much more successful for telling a story about the species,” said Tobias. “Telling a story between the viewer and the animal is really powerful for conservation.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht A large part of their aim is to introduce the world to the 33 small wild cat species that are relatively unknown, so more can be done to protect them. “If you protect small cats, you protect big cats,” she added. The pair also wants to prove humans can coexist with big and small wild cats. “There are lots of human activities that might negatively impact cats without people knowing,” Tobias said. “People want to protect natural spaces and help with coexistence.” View this post on Instagram In Paraguay at the time of this writing, the team has had camera traps set up since April to capture the northern oncilla, with a ground crew frequently checking on them, but the cat has remained elusive. View this post on Instagram “It’s been pretty incredible,” Kennerknecht said, “but measuring local awareness has been tough.” They’ve set up billboards in areas with wild cats, featuring pictures of the local cats with the slogan, “I’m your neighbor.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht As for their favorite species, Kennerknecht said his is a bobcat, as that’s the feline that launched his photographic journey in Santa Cruz. But for Tobias: “There’s nothing more beautiful than a female leopard.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Below are the cats they’ve photographed so far: Lion — Zambia Jaguar — Brazil Tiger — India Snow Leopard — Kyrgyzstan Leopard — Zambia Mainland Clouded Leopard — Malaysia Sunda Clouded Leopard — Malaysia African Golden Cat — Uganda Caracal — Yemen Serval — Tanzania Geoffroy’s Cat — Argentina Southern Oncila — Brazil Andean Mountain Cat- Argentina Pampas Cat- Bolivia Ocelot — Panama Margay — Panama Marbled Cat — Malaysia Borneo Bay Cat — Malaysia Asiatic Golden Cat — Indonesia Bobcat — U.S. Canada Lynx — Canada Eurasian Lynx — Kyrgyzstan Iberian Lynx — Spain Mountain Lion — Chile Cheetah — Tanzania Mainland Leopard Cat — Malaysia Sunda Leopard Cat — Malaysia Flat-Headed Cat — Malaysia Rusty-Spotted Cat — India Fishing Cat — Thailand Pallas’s Cat — Mongolia Jungle Cat — India Sand Cat — Western Sahara Black-footed Cat — South Africa European Wild Cat — Spain Afro-Asiatic Wild Cat — Botswana Chinese Mountain Cat — China Jaguarundi — Location Unconfirmed/South America Güiña — Location Unconfirmed/Chile/Argentina This article was originally written by William Ormes Roder for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Life is a little easier now for a southern ground hornbill in the Netherlands, thanks to 3D-printed prostheses for his upper and lower beak. The turkey-sized bird at the ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo suffered a severe injury that broke both sections of his bill and left him with two stumps, making it difficult for him to pick up food and groom himself. “He managed reasonably well with them, but he could no longer do everything a hornbill naturally does,” ARTIS veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout said in a press release . To improve his well-being, the team perfected custom prostheses that are “virtually identical” to his original beak. “A bird uses its beak all day long, to pick up food and, for example, to preen its plumage. Especially with a young bird that can still live to a very old age, we felt it was important to see if we could improve its quality of life,” van Zijll Langhout added. ARTIS Although several birds have been fitted with artificial beaks, this hornbill is believed to be the first to receive replacements for both the upper and lower beak. Should the beak parts continue to function well for the long-term, the team plans to publish a scientific paper detailing exactly how they created the prostheses, so veterinarians around the world can help similar patients. The process is technically complex, as every bird has a unique beak that perfectly aligns to its skull and other anatomy. If the shape isn’t exactly right for either part of the bill, the animal will struggle to use the prosthesis. To ensure their creation would be a success, van Zijll Langhout and her colleagues performed a CT scan of the bird’s head as well as the broken beak pieces. The prostheses were then 3D-printed from plastic, and orthopedic surgeons meticulously attached them using titanium components. View this post on Instagram One of the biggest risks with a procedure like this is that the bird will reject the new beak, which could result in the animal refusing to eat. The zoo staff planned for that possibility and were prepared to have the prostheses removed if need be — but so far, all is going well: The team reported the bird settled in right away after the beak attachment operation and even appeared to be “smiling” afterward . And the day following the surgery, he began eating independently. “That was an incredibly important moment for us,” said van Zijll Langhout. “He understood that he could use his beak and began to discover for himself what was possible with it.” RELATED: From a Dolphin’s Tail to a Bird’s Beak: 7 Innovative Prosthetics That Have Helped Animals

items.descriptionOriginal: The treatment delivers a light-sensitive algae protein to the retina. Paired with special goggles, it can restore limited vision and lasts for years. The patients sit perfectly still as a needle inches toward one of their eyes. After the injection, they’ll no longer be completely human. The syringe is filled with a gene therapy that installs a light-sensitive algae protein into failing retinas and could reboot some lost vision. When scientists first proposed using algae proteins to restore human eyesight, the idea seemed like science fiction. Could alien proteins integrate into our intricate visual system? Even if they did, could the brain translate the resulting signals into sight, rather than nonsensical bursts of light? A new study suggests yes, with caveats. The team treated people with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that gradually destroys light-sensing cells in the retina. Seven of ten patients showed improved light sensitivity. After patients donned goggles that deliver pulses of light to activate the algae proteins, the team tested their eyesight. Roughly half could reach for and touch objects or identify the orientation of a black bar, a common test of visual recovery. The treatment is still far from restoring full vision. What patients saw was too blurry and the field of view too narrow to discern texture or fine detail. The boundaries of objects looked squiggly. But those who responded to the treatment continued to improve over roughly five years. One participant, whose story made headlines in 2021 , can now recognize and count different objects, and white stripes on a crosswalk pop out. The study, called PIONEER , is an ambitious clinical trial combining gene therapy with optogenetics. The first goal was to assess safety, and it met the mark. Most participants experienced a brief bout of inflammation in the eye receiving the injection. The only patient to suffer a severe side effect was quickly treated with medication. The findings suggest the initial success wasn’t a fluke. The study “represents an important milestone for optogenetic vision restoration,” said study author Stefan Futterknecht at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, in a press release . Setting Sights High Around two decades ago, Karl Deisseroth was hunting for new ways to control brain cells. Electrical bursts and chemicals, which are how neurons communicate, seemed like obvious choices. But nature had something stranger to offer: algae. Algae produce a protein called channelrhodopsin. When activated by light, the protein changes neuron activity using a mechanism that works similarly in mammalian cells. In a foundational paper , Deisseroth’s team inserted the protein into rodent neurons, and voilá—the neurons could now be controlled using light. The technology, called optogenetics, revolutionized neuroscience. By genetically tagging specific neurons with channelrhodopsin, scientists can now dial the cells’ activity up or down like a dimmer switch. Optogenetic experiments have revealed brain circuits that shape feelings, memory, and cognition with unprecedented precision. Researchers panning for more genes in different algae strains struck gold again. One channelrhodopsin variant they found, ChrimsonR, was particularly exciting. Unlike the classic version that’s activated by blue light, ChrimsonR responds to amber light, which penetrates tissues better and is less damaging. More recently, scientists have begun to use generative AI to redesign natural proteins to make them even more sensitive to light. “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, when the technology won the coveted prize this year. Still, it has mainly been considered a research tool. Light It Up Retinitis pigmentosa gradually robs people of their eyesight. Researchers have linked over 100 genetic variations to the condition, which kills off light-sensitive cells in the retina. “The replacement (or editing) of a single gene would not help most persons,” wrote Deisseroth in the New England Journal of Medicine . Instead, adding channelrhodopsin could offer a more universal solution by rewiring surviving neurons. Early successes bolstered the idea. In one study , scientists equipped cones—a type of retinal light-sensing cell—with channelrhodopsin in mice with retinitis pigmentosa. The therapy boosted their light sensitivity. It also reactivated cones that had stopped responding to light in human retina samples. The new study took a different approach. In advanced disease, cones may have already degenerated beyond the point at which they could be saved. So instead, the gene therapy targeted ganglion cells. These cells process signals from light-sensitive cells and pass that information to the brain, but don’t detect light themselves. Ganglion cells are, however, more resilient than cones. Add channelrhodopsin, and they could become substitute light sensors. The team packed genetic instructions for ChrimsonR into a harmless viral delivery system and injected it into the poorer seeing eye of 10 patients aged 40 to 73. All were legally blind, and each received one of three escalating doses. As the patients gradually built up levels of the algae protein in their eyes, the team faced another challenge: Translating visual scenes from the outside world into amber light that the engineered ganglion cells could recognize. They developed specialized goggles that look a bit like Apple’s Vision Pro. The goggles use a camera to scan the field of view thousands of times per second, monitoring for light changes in every pixel. When the device detects a change, it pulses amber light from that pixel into the eye. Because our eyes naturally dart around—often without us noticing—this dynamic method may better mimic normal vision. With the goggles on, 6 of 10 participants showed clinically meaningful improvement in light sensitivity, with more than a fourfold boost over baseline readings. One participant improved over 62-fold. Of the eight who agreed to further eyesight tests, roughly half could touch a notebook, grab a small staple box, and detect changes in a rotating bar. Of those who initially responded to the treatment, improvements lasted for years. Their brains also seemed to adapt to the alien light sensors. In one test, participants were asked to open or close their eyes while looking at a tumbler. Electrical brain signals related to vision were more coherent with eyes open, suggesting their perception depended on improved visual input. Any gene therapy carries risk. In an already worsening eye, inflammation and other side effects could cause further damage. Overall, the injection appeared relatively safe. Most participants experienced a temporary increase in eye pressure, but no detectable side effects throughout the body. The retina’s overall structure remained unchanged. One person suffered a blockage in a major eye artery that cleared within minutes after treatment with an FDA-approved eye drop. For now, the participants still can’t read or see faces. The therapy reaches only a fraction of their ganglion cells, making sharper vision harder to restore. More advanced versions of channelrhodopsin with greater light sensitivity may increase resolution. As for the hardware, the team is working on versions of the goggles that deliver more accurate and timely stimulation. Potential upgrades include an eye tracker, software to preprocess visual scenes, and even holographs . “Overall, although optogenetic methods have been developed primarily for basic science discovery,” wrote Deisseroth, they’re now heading towards “diverse therapeutic approaches.” The post Blind Patients Recover Partial Vision in Gene Therapy Trial appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips Reading Time: 3 minutes Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips If you’re wondering, “Where can I buy peppermint oil in bulk?”, you have many options, including specialist wholesalers, ingredient distributors, and online marketplaces. Wholesale Botanics, Bulk Apothecary, and Bulk Natural Oils are just a few options worth considering. Walmart also lists larger bottles, while Amazon is another marketplace to check. The best starting point depends on the quantity of the product you need. A larger bottle may suit occasional soap making, but regular production calls for a reliable supplier. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Specialist Suppliers for Bulk Peppermint Oil Consider these suppliers if you’re looking to buy peppermint oil in bulk. Wholesale Botanics Wholesale Botanics lists peppermint oil in 5, 25, 100, and 400-pound sizes, with custom quotes for larger quantities. Buyers have the option to choose between Mentha piperita and Mentha arvensis variants. Wholesale Botanics’ essential oil wholesale service offers consultations and sample packs, enabling you to discuss requirements before placing an order. You can also request a sample of the variant you want to purchase and confirm that testing documents are also provided. Bulk Apothecary Bulk Apothecary offers Japanese and Supreme peppermint oils in 5, 25, and 400-pound options. Shipping is calculated at checkout, so bear that in mind when purchasing. The smaller bottles allow you to test a variety before moving to a larger order. It helps to ask the company’s team about quantities beyond the listed options. New Directions Aromatics New Directions Aromatics offers its Peppermint Essential Oil (Supreme) in sizes that extend up to 396 pounds. This is the Mentha piperita variation, but it also has organic peppermint listings. Availability and dispatch arrangements differ between sizes, so it helps to confirm the selected pack is available. Bulk Natural Oils Bulk Natural Oils offer Piperita and Arvensis peppermint oils as well as organic options. The website lists a minimum spend of $150 on a combination of products. This option might suit businesses purchasing several ingredients together. Shay and Company Shay and Company is a good choice for smaller buys as it offers peppermint oil in smaller bottles in 5- and 10-pound sizes. Orders over 25 pounds require an email inquiry. Its Willamette Valley listing identifies Oregon as the origin, making it worth exploring when sourcing location matters to your product. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Can You Buy on Amazon or Walmart? Walmart’s online listings include peppermint oil in 16-ounce bottles as well as one-gallon containers. This might suit smaller projects that don’t have a large wholesale commitment. Ensure that you check the individual seller, ingredients, and documentation instead of relying on the retailer’s name alone. If you want to purchase peppermint oil on Amazon, search for the quantity you need and check who sells and ships the product. Double-check that the listing describes essential oil and not fragrance oil, extract, or a diluted blend. Check the Oil Before Comparing Prices You would typically come across two main variants: Mentha piperita, which is peppermint, and Mentha arvensis, commonly called cornmint or Japanese peppermint. While both appear in peppermint ranges, their aromas and chemical profiles differ. Make sure that you match the botanical name to your formula instead of substituting whichever costs less. Where possible, request a certificate of analysis, an available batch-specific GC/MS report, and a safety data sheet. These cover specifications, handling hazards, and chemical composition. Request the relevant certification and confirmation of suitability for certified organic, food, or oral care application. Remember that “pure” alone doesn’t establish that an oil meets your requirements. Compare Delivered Cost and Order Size In your comparison between products, factor in shipping, taxes, import charges, and membership fees. Check whether the ounces refer to weight or fluid volume. For international orders, check that the selected quantity can actually be shipped to your country and clearly establish who pays the customs charges. Drum deliveries can involve freight shipping, so ask about unloading requirements as well. For occasional purchases, compare membership savings with subscription costs before signing up for a wholesale plan. Always test a sample in the finished product before scaling up, as peppermint oil can irritate skin, and cosmetics and candles require appropriate safety or performance testing. Confirm lead times, return conditions, and remaining shelf life before paying. Store the oil tightly sealed, away from heat and light, and order only what you can realistically use. Choosing Where to Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk Amazon and Walmart are worth exploring if you want to purchase a large bottle as a one-time thing. For regular production, specialist suppliers give you more options to discuss specifications and quantities. Start by requesting a sample and a quote for the oil you need. Once you test it in your formula, you can decide whether the pricing, documentation, and availability make it a practical choice for future orders. The post Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: At 74, she decided to learn something new. Today, at 82, she rides a bike, drives a tractor and shares her adventures on social media! Sukhma’s journey began when a joke turned into a secret learning adventure between her and a family member. Away from the rest of the family, they practised together until she finally learnt to ride. Eight years later, she’s doing much more than riding a bike. She drives a tractor and runs her own social media page, sharing reels of herself riding. She didn’t learn because she had to. She learnt because she wanted to. Sukhma’s story reminds us that curiosity has no expiry date, and age doesn’t have to stop us from trying something we’ve always wanted to do. items.descriptionOriginal: From being body-shamed in school to starring in a Netflix special, Sumukhi Suresh is turning the judgements women face into comedy. She gave up dancing for fear of being laughed at, but eventually found her voice through stand-up comedy. She went on to create and star in Pushpavalli and create Motormouth to make more space for women’s stories. In her Netflix special Hoemonal, Sumukhi tackles body image, dating, being single and the societal pressure on women to become mothers. Through humour, she brings conversations often brushed under the carpet into the spotlight, challenging the expectations women are constantly asked to live up to. Her journey is a reminder that you don’t have to shrink yourself to fit into someone else’s idea of who you should be. Sometimes, the most powerful way to challenge judgement is to laugh at it, speak up and tell your story on your own terms. What do you think women are judged unfairly for the most: their bodies, their age or being single? Tell us in the comments! #SumukhiSuresh #Hoemonal #StandUpComedy #BodyShaming #WomenInComedy #IndianComedy #BodyPositivity #SheTheChange #thebetterindia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in Spain have shown that a modular tire in which tread and casing are designed as separate pieces stays together while in use, provided that it’s properly inflated. “This is an encouraging step toward a more sustainable tire architecture, where the worn tread could potentially be replaced while the main tire structure is reused,” says study team member Farshad Afshari , a PhD researcher at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM).. A modular automobile tire could be easier to recycle compared to conventional ones, which require time- and labor-intensive separation of rubber treads and sidewalls from steel belts and bead cores. It would also use materials more efficiently, since there would be less material to replace at any given time. A modular tire could also be better for the environment . Conventional rubber tires are a prominent source of microplastic pollution because tiny rubber particles degrade due to friction and enter the air and waterways. But the modular design could open up the possibility of making each component of the tire from safer and more easily recyclable materials. It’s a compelling idea in theory, but would the components of a modular tire actually stay together in practice? Afshari and his collaborators built a scaled-down prototype of their ECOTIRE modular tire concept, in which tread and casing are mechanically interlocked through a series of bumps and hollows like the two halves of a waffle iron. They tested the tire on a custom-built rolling test rig in the lab to see how the tire would fare while varying parameters such as load, turning radius, inflation pressure, and slip. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree Reading Time: 3 minutes Greening upwind of cities may offer a simple fix for urban heat, with new research showing strategically placed suburban forests can cool more than half a metropolitan area. Greening upwind of cities draws on a centuries-old planning idea. Researchers behind the new study found inspiration in traditional Chinese village design , where settlements were built backed by mountains, facing water, and surrounded by forest. That layout, known as the mountain-water-forest framework, helped villages stay naturally cooler. Shi-Jie Cao, director of the Center for Sustainable Built Environment at Southeast University in Nanjing, led the team exploring whether this ancient pattern could work for modern megacities. Many cities have already tried planting trees within urban cores to combat heat. Results have often fallen short, leaving some cities sweltering through increasingly hot summers despite those efforts. Cao’s team wondered if location mattered more than volume. Placing vegetation strategically outside a city, rather than scattering it inside, might produce better cooling results. Testing that idea required a different approach than simply counting trees planted downtown. Researchers built a computer model to simulate temperature changes in urban cores during hot summer days. They tested what would happen if suburban land upwind of two Chinese cities, Beijing and Shanghai, were converted into either forest or built-up development. The two cities offered contrasting geography, with Beijing sitting on a plain near mountains and Shanghai positioned along the coast. Results revealed a clear mechanism. Greening upwind of cities creates a mass of cooler air in the surrounding suburbs. Prevailing winds then carry that cooler air directly into the city, lowering temperatures across the urban core without requiring any changes inside city limits. Encouraged by these findings, researchers expanded their analysis to six additional megacities worldwide. Cairo, Kinshasa, São Paulo, Houston, Sydney, and London each represent vastly different climates and urban layouts. Testing across such varied conditions helped determine whether the cooling strategy held up beyond China’s borders. Across all eight cities studied, greening upwind of cities produced an average cooling effect of 0.4 degrees Celsius. That temperature drop applied across at least half of each city’s total area during peak summer heat. Exact results varied by location, but the underlying cooling pathway remained consistent everywhere researchers tested it. A city skyline rises beyond green suburban land, illustrating the wind pathway researchers studied when greening upwind of cities to reduce heat. Photo by Andy Lee on Pexels. Shanghai’s results illustrated the strategy’s limits alongside its potential. Cooling effects there were more modest and localized than in Beijing. Shanghai’s cooling sea breezes simply don’t align well with the areas where suburban trees could realistically be planted, reducing how effectively wind carries cooled air into the city. That finding carries an important caveat for city planners. Cao emphasized that this approach isn’t a blanket call for planting trees everywhere possible. Success depends on cities having consistent wind patterns and available space specifically positioned upwind of urban centers. Available space presents its own complication in many real-world settings. Suburban land upwind of major cities often already hosts housing developments, roads, and industrial facilities. Implementing this strategy would require creative, multi-functional land-use planning rather than simply clearing space for new forests. Local governments and other stakeholders would need to coordinate closely to make such changes possible. Getting buy-in across multiple jurisdictions and property owners adds real-world complexity that no climate model can capture. Political and logistical hurdles may prove just as challenging as the science itself. Beyond the specific temperature findings, Cao pointed to a broader lesson drawn from traditional village design. Cities benefit from thinking about vegetation, wind, topography, and water as one interconnected system rather than isolated green spaces scattered without coordination. That systems-level thinking represents a meaningful shift from how most urban cooling efforts currently operate. As global temperatures continue rising, cities will likely need every available tool to manage heat exposure for residents. Greening upwind of cities offers city planners a research-backed strategy that works with existing wind patterns rather than against them. The approach won’t work everywhere, but where geography cooperates, it could meaningfully ease the burden of urban heat without requiring dramatic changes to how city centers themselves are built. The post Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree appeared first on Happy Eco News .
